We were on this item yesterday and there was quite a bit of misunderstanding about it. This was and still is a luxury tax, although the government call it something else; they call it an excise tax now. They have reduced it from 25 per cent to 10 per cent. When we were talking about this matter yesterday afternoon, before we adjourned for the day, we were mentioning only the 10 per cent tax. But at that time we forgot to take into consideration the fact that in this provision we should cover also the sales tax. On an article that costs say $100, you have the sales tax, and you have your 10 per cent excise tax on top of that, which makes the price $118. That is the price at which the manufacturer sells to the wholesaler. In most cases the wholesaler takes a markup of not more than about 25 per cent; therefore he adds to the $18 tax his 25 per cent, which brings it up to $22.50. The wholesaler in turn sells to the retailer, and most retailers take a margin of about 50 per cent. So the 50 per cent is added to the $22.50, and poor old John public has to pay $33.75 to enable the treasury to collect this $18 tax that the government has imposed on each $100 worth of goods. It is no wonder that the cost of living has gone up, with things of this kind happening. I feel this tax should be abolished.

One other point was brought to my attention. I described the four main groups of goods in this country now, so far as taxation is concerned: the first group, on which no sales tax was levied; the second group, everything else on which sales tax was levied; the third group, on which a 10 per cent excise tax was levied in addition, and finally, the liquor and tobacco group, which has always had a traditionally high tax. There is one other small group covered by schedule IV of the act, which provides that goods made by either the institute for the blind or by deaf and dumb schools are subject to only half the sales tax.

To go a little further in this matter: as I said before, the manufacturer's price, let us say, is $100. He adds the 8 per cent sales tax, and the 10 per cent luxury tax brings the tax up to $18, which makes the wholesaler's price $118. The wholesaler's margin is 25 per cent; therefore to that $118 is added his $29.50, which brings up the retailer's cost to $147.50. The retailer makes a margin of 50 per cent, which adds another $73.75, which brings the price of a $100 article up to $221.25 to the public. That is why I say this tax should be done away with.

I should like to say a word in reply to the hon. member who has just referred to the profits made by retailers. Evidently the hon. member, who has built up a case on the basis of an increase from $100 to $221.25, is not at all familiar with retail practice. I doubt very much whether any hon. member who has spoken on this question has dealt with it from a real knowledge of merchandising. I want to say definitely that it was a good move to change the 25 per cent excise tax to 10 per cent. It was a good move because it made possible the purchase of luggage and many other articles that do not come within the scope of luxury items. More than that, the 25 per cent profits tax never had a profit added to it. It meant nothing to the retailer except additional worry to collect the tax and pass it along. It also prevented the sale of luggage to many customers who required it.
When the hon. member takes $100 and adds an 8 per cent sales tax to it, he is doing what is right. The manufacturers charge and collect an 8 per cent sales tax for the government. In addition they collect a special 10 per cent excise tax for the government. The retailer does not make any profit or markup whatsoever on that $18.
Certainly he does.

It is all very well for the hon. member, who does not know what he is talking about, to say that he does. The fact remains that no reliable firm in Canada will put a markup on that 10 per cent. I venture to make that assertion here today.
In addition to that, the hon. member first adds $18 to the manufacturer's price; then he puts 25 per cent on that, which makes $29.50. I do not know where he gets the 25 per cent. Then he adds another 50 per cent. The average retailer adds to his first cost what is considered a reasonable markup to make it possible for him to pay his rent and overhead expenses, including help. That figure is anywhere from 23 per cent to 29 per cent, depending on the type of business. After he has paid all his expenses, the net profit remaining to him, roughly speaking, amounts to anywhere from 3| per cent to 6 or 7 per cent. That is the story. That applies to most reliable retailers throughout Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. It is quite true that there is the odd case-the hon. member does not indicate a thing by shaking his head. He may shake it one way or the other. He may shake it up or down, but these are the facts. I wanted to say this word in fairness to the retailers throughout Canada.

The hon. member has been in business for a long time. I do not know what his practice is, but let us suppose he bought an article on which there was a hidden tax, and he paid $100 for that article. Suppose he asked the wholesaler how much tax was included in the price, and the answer was $18; he would not say: I will mark it down $18 and then take my profit on the figure thus arrived at. That is not the way business is done. The figures I gave are not my own figures. They are from retailers from coast to coast, from Halifax to Victoria. They are figures obtained from over 3,700 people.

Would the hon. member be good enough not to quote a hundred or twenty-five or ten or eleven, but just one? Give us the figures of one retailer from Halifax. Give us the name of one firm. That is all I am asking.

I am interested in the people and what they pay in hidden taxes. The leader of this group had something to say on that yesterday afternoon, and I fully support him in what he said. I believe the people of Canada have a right to know what they are paying in taxes every time they buy an article or whenever they do business.
I do not smoke. I understand that those who do smoke pay a lot of taxes that they do not know they are paying. I understand that if they buy a package of cigarette papers the actual price of the papers may be three cents, and there is an additional ten cents which is a tax. I do not know whether they know that or not, but I contend that on every package of cigarette papers it should be indicated that the buyer is charged ten cents for the privilege of rolling his own, and that that ten cents goes to the government.
If I had my way I would insist that on every price tag the actual price of the goods should be marked, and, in addition, the amount of tax imposed. I believe that was done in some instances during the war. We in this corner of the house believe that it is not necessary to tax to the extent that governments do today. I am not going into that now. We have said that over the past fifteen years. We believe that a substantial proportion of the money that is used by governments today could be obtained by methods other than taxing or borrowing. Be that as it may, it does seem to me that the power of money manipulation works in the dark. There is no question about that; otherwise there would not be the ignorance that there is in the country concerning money.
I do not know whether I heard a hee-haw coming from the other side of the house, but even the type of creation that uses such an expression does not understand very much about money. Holy Writ warns us about the hidden things of darkness. I believe that some of these things should be brought to light. There may be some reason to suspect that those who operate this vicious and yet powerful system would want some things hidden. The idea is not to let people know too much about it, so the tax is hidden.

-as though it might have been cut from the corner of a $20 bill. I read it and I find it bears the imprint: "20 cigarettes". I do not know whether a person buying cigarettes would insist every time he bought them upon being informed that he is buying twenty of them. Surely he would understand that. What he does not know is the amount of tax he is paying on that package of cigarettes.
My leader tells me that the man who buys cigarettes is paying 29 cents in taxes every time he buys a package. Instead of a small stamp bearing the imprint "20 cigarettes" I say it should bear the words: Your government is now taxing you 29 cents on this package of cigarettes. In this way the tax would not be hidden from the eyes of those who smoke the things within the package. The blame for the tax should be placed squarely on the shoulders of the government imposing it. People should not be left under the impression that it is the manufacturer who imposes the tax-and there may be some who have that impression.
I am serious in what I say. During the war it was provided by certain regulations of the wartime prices and trade board-and if in any details I am wrong, I shall stand corrected-that, in order to have fair business practice in the fur trade, any fur when advertised had to be properly described as to the type of fur used. It was not good enough to say, "This is muskrat"-because it may not have been muskrat; it may have been tomcat. In advertising the fur the advertiser had to state the type of fur being used; if it was dyed rabbit, it had to be so stated. Under that regulation which, in my view, was a good one, people knew what they were buying. No one will gainsay that.
The same should apply in connection with taxes. People should know how much they are paying in taxes and how much for the actual article. I urge therefore that we do away with hidden taxes. Believe me, if people knew every time they spent a dollar here or there how much of it went for taxes it would not be long before they would be aroused to the necessity of some type of monetary reform.
They would stop blaming private enterprise then.

Mr. Chairman, there is no specific item under which I could mention the commodity I should like to bring to the attention of the committee, because it is not

one of the commodities from which the tax has been removed. I wish, however, to protest against the tax on ice cream.
Resolution No. 5 would be the proper one.
Carried.
No, the resolution is not carried.
The hon. member is out of order if he attempts to discuss a sales tax on the excise tax item. I suggest that he wait until we reach resolution 5.
I am asking the Chairman for his ruling.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I suggest that the hon. member wait until we are discussing resolution 5.

I agree with the hon. member for Peterborough West and disagree with the senior member for Halifax. After all, I believe I learned to disagree with the senior member for Halifax when some years ago I used to listen to the leaders of the party to which he belongs. In those days-and I argued the same way; I admit it-the imposition of a tariff was always alleged to be an imposition on the public, because it was not the tariff that the people paid but the pyramided price at the retail end, at which stage the cost price included the original cost and the tariff in the first instance, with at every stage the additional amount of profit added to both the original value and the tariff, and pyramided profits on both.
I think this is perfectly true with regard to the tax we are discussing today. Yesterday the parliamentary assistant referred to the dollar article with the 10 per cent tax on it, which, of course, amounted to ten cents. Then he used an extravagant markup, which is not generally used, but which I shall use because it makes a simple computation-and we reach the point where we have one dollar becoming two dollars. The 10 per cent, it is true, is 20 cents on the two dollars. But as a matter of fact when you compute the markup you are not paying 10 per cent on the two dollars, but rather 20 per cent on the original dollar-which is a different thing, indeed.
The only difference is that in one case the government gets the whole tax, and in the other case the public pays it and it is distributed to the wholesaler, the jobber, the retailer or whomever it may be. The difficulty is that the consumer pays and the government actually loses revenue in that way. I agree with the hon. member from the Social Credit group who has just spoken when he states that these things should be made known to the public.

I know that in British Columbia, Saskatchewan and other provinces where they have had sales taxes, there have been outcries against sales taxes to the extent of two or three per cent, forgetting all about the federal sales tax of 8 per cent and all the other hidden taxes. We never heard anything about that-and the strange feature of it all is that supporters of the Liberal party	are	the most violent
critics of provincial sales taxes, when they are collected directly from the public in amounts of two or three per cent-despite the fact that the federal tax imposed by the government they support is many times that large.
I agree, therefore, that these taxes should be stated to the extent we can have them stated. I do not like the idea of changing the present tax at the retail end to one at the manufacturer's end.

There is one suggestion I would pass on to the parliamentary assistant which might be followed up by his department. I believe all the discussions thus far on sales and excise taxes indicate that there ought to be some source from which members of the House of Commons can obtain authentic information as to the portion of the consumer price which in reality is taxation imposed by this or other governments, and that portion which is legitimate cost. A good many attempts have been made by associations such as the retail merchants' association to compute the effect of excise and sales taxes on consumer cost. I suspect that some of the figures given by the hon. member for Peterborough West came from such a source. If they are not correct-
They are correct.

I am only saying that if they are not correct, surely it is necessary that there should be placed at the disposal of agencies of that kind information that will make it possible for them to get the correct figures. I am aware of certain investigations that have been carried on in the United States, and calculations founded on fact indicate that up to 86 per cent of the consumer cost of a gallon of oil used in the transmission of an automobile consists of taxation imposed by either the state or the federal government, mainly the federal government. On a pair of denim overalls used by a farmer, up to 70 per cent of the consumer price consists of taxes imposed at various levels in manufacturing and distribution.
When they are pyramided.

When they are pyramided. I think the parliamentary assistant could do this committee a service by making available
Excise Tax Act
these figures in connection with certain of the common articles used by the people of Canada from day to day, so that the consumer may know exactly what is tax and what is legitimate cost.

I should like to bring up the matter of portable sprinkler irrigation systems. I referred to this in the debate on the address, and requested that when the budget resolutions were brought down provision be made for removing the tax on this type of farm equipment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That would come under resolution 5.
I will take it up under No. 5.

I want to protest against the continuance of the 10 per cent tax under 3 (a), on trunks, suitcases, bags and luggage of all kinds. We are thankful that this war tax is being reduced from 35 to 10 per cent, but these articles are not luxury items and there should be no tax at all. This industry was imposed upon during the war to a greater extent than any such industry in the country.
In my constituency there is a small industry which started from limited beginnings but has grown to a fair size. Of course, it cannot compare with the large industries in the country, because it does not manufacture a full range, its products being only staple items. During the war a tax of 35 per cent was imposed upon the products of this industry. I doubt if there is a member of the house or a household in the country without a trunk, a suitcase, a bag, or luggage of some kind. Therefore I submit these articles are a necessity. I cannot understand why they should be classed with ash trays, tobacco pipes, smokers' accessories, and luxuries.
This tax cannot be justified, particularly in view of the recent devaluation of the pound sterling, which creates serious competition for this industry. Has the department taken into consideration this additional competition which the industry in my constituency and other such industries throughout Canada will have to contend against? Articles are coming into this country under a 20 per cent preference and are taking business from industries of this kind.
I consider this an unfair, unreasonable and unjust tax, and I do not believe it should be continued. If it were in order I would move that this 10 per cent tax on trunks, suitcases, bags and luggage of all kinds be deleted from the resolution.

I should like to associate myself with the hon. member for Cumberland in the representations he has made for the elimination of the 10 per cent tax on luggage. I do

Excise Tax Act
not do this because I am a retailer selling luggage, but rather because I feel that this industry should not receive this treatment. I want to emphasize the point made by the hon. member, that this tax places the Canadian manufacturer of luggage in an unfavourable position owing to the devaluation of the pound. A large quantity of English leather goods is coming into Canada, and with the devaluation of the pound the competition is going to be that much keener and the Canadian manufacturer will be placed in an unfair position.
The firm to which the hon. member referred, Christie Trunk and Bag Company, Limited, is a fine company which is making a good article. They are in competition with the rest of Canada, and I am anxious to see them maintain their position and continue on a fair competitive basis.
May I say to the hon. member for Cumberland that I was one of those who went to the government last year to make representations to have the 35 per cent tax reduced to the present 10 per cent. Of course we asked for the complete elimination of the tax.
For the benefit of those who do not know how this business is handled, may I say that in the case of luggage the price ticket states the tax. There is no hidden tax such as has been referred to by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Everything is distinctly marked on the price ticket, and prices are more or less set by the manufacturer.
Let me say in fairness to retailers, not just those in Halifax but in British Columbia and throughout the whole dominion-
We were not criticizing the retailer.
The hon. member started out to criticize them.
No.
No, we did not. We were criticizing the government.
Order.

We can read what was said. I think I can follow an argument as well as the average person. Hon. members certainly tried to contend that the retailer was selling at an excessive profit, due largely to the pyramiding of the taxes. That is the position in which they try to place retailers. I want to defend the retailer and say that on the whole-and there are a great many of them throughout Canada- they are trying to carry on the same fine type of business that is carried on by other trades. I think it is safe to say that because of wartime restrictions the retailer today is making less profit than he ever made
(Mr. Isnor.]
before. I do not know whether hon. members who criticize retailers, including the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar-
I rise on a question of privilege. We have not criticized retailers.
No one has.
No one has. If the retailer pays out $1.25 he is entitled under our present system to a profit on his investment based on $1.25. We are not complaining about that.
You have a man of straw there.
If the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is withdrawing his argument, it is all right with me.
No; he did not withdraw his argument.
You just do not understand.
The hon. member says the member for Rosetown-Biggar does not understand. I agree with him.
What is that?
No; it was you who did not understand.
The hon. member for Halifax did not understand.
I am sorry, but the hon. member for Halifax does not seem to understand anything.
He does not even understand what he is saying himself.
I am most willing to be taught at any time. I have done fairly well in the retail business and made a profit in a fair legitimate way.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: At 25 per cent or 50 per cent?
I was about to say that today retailers are carrying on with a closer margin than ever before.
That is right.
We all agree with that.
You can criticize them as much as you wish-
Nobody criticized them.

You may also criticize the price setting plan, but there are a great many manufactured lines today in which the retail price is more or less suggested to the retailer. The retail price is closer to cost than it ever was before. I think I should set hon. members right as to that. That is all I care to say at this time.

I wish to support what the hon. member tor Cumberland has said about the excise tax. He forgets, however, that departmental officials throughout the country will interpret the word "accessories". Having certain powers, rights and privileges, they will notify the various excise collectors what to do. The resolution may be passed in the twinkling of an eye, but departmental officials will write something different into the resolution. They can make rules and regulations apart from it. I think we should be most careful about the language that is used. I have seen examples in the city of Toronto of what happens, and I have had many complaints from retail merchants and others engaged in this kind of business. They say that they have great difficulty, and that there are different interpretations made in various places. We should clarify the matter, because if the committee passes the resolution it means it will be enforced in some places and not in others. There will be different interpretations. The department will interpret the word "accessories" as meaning something that was never intended by the resolution.

As to the statement made by the senior member for Halifax, I should like to say that I have been in business in one way or another for the past seventeen years. Some day I hope to have the privilege of going to Halifax and watching the hon. member work out his profit. During all the time I have been in business I have never been accused of nefarious practices. When an article costs me $1.25 I have always figured my profit on a cost of $1.25. There is no man in business in Canada today who has the time to check over all the statutes of Canada to figure out how much he has been charged in taxes, and take that off before he figures his profit.
Not even the hon. member for Halifax.
Not even the hon. member for Halifax. If an article costs a man $1.25, he is entitled to his profit on that $1.25.
Would this be the appropriate time to inquire from the parliamentary assistant what the excise taxes are on tobaccos in various forms?
The hon. member can find that in the Excise Act. None of these resolutions pertain to tobacco or spirits.
You will tie up the Christmas trade. You will not be able to get your goods out of customs.

I should like to ask the
parliamentary assistant if under the old law the retail purchase tax was 25 per cent on 45781-103
Excise Tax Act
the retail price. They have made a pretty smart move. They have removed the 25 per cent tax because the public demanded it, and now they are making the manufacturer and importer collect the tax, and are hiding it so that nobody will know anything about it. Like other hon. members, I think that the tax should be shown so that people will know exactly what they are paying. The same applies to the sales tax. If the amount of the sales tax had to be shown on each article purchased, there would not be any sales tax today because people would be so much annoyed. You would need so many votes over there that you would take the sales tax off.

I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant about the suggestion I made a few minutes ago. Does he not think that full information should be made available so that members of the house might know exactly what the situation is?

I was advised yesterday that I was too eager to answer questions, and I was waiting until each resolution was fairly well completed to answer the points which have been raised. As to the question of the hon. member for Peace River, whether it would be practicable to have the sum total of all taxes shown on every item-
Not on every one-on a representative group.
The hon. member says "not on every one"; but where is he to draw the line?
Take a representative group.
The principal taxes in Canada, on the federal level, are personal income tax, corporation tax, and excise tax.
I am speaking of hidden taxes.

The hon. member accused me of being too eager yesterday; now he is somewhat eager himself. In the final tax fraction of the cost of an article these hidden taxes are embodied. Property tax is paid by the factory that made the article, also corporation taxes and provincial taxes on that level. All these are represented in the cost of the article. If you want to know where the federal taxes are to be found that the people of Canada pay, in the Excise Act there is specific information as to where taxes are levied.
The next point raised was about the matter of markups. I agree with the hon. member for Halifax that there has been a great change in opinion on the other side of the house between yesterday and this afternoon. We heard that when the government put the

Excise Tax Act
tax on the manufacturer's level, the wholesaler, the jobber and the retailer were able to pyramid it, and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said that the retailer added these extra taxes on the retail level. There was a complete change when the hon. member for Halifax suggested there was an implication that retailers were taking advantage of these taxes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: When he misrepresented what had been said.

Let me say a few words about the actual form that these taxes take. If we had price control in Canada, and had definitely allotted markups, as we did under price control, then the arguments made would have been true, although even then we exempted taxes from these markups. Today we have not price control. The actual markups of the retail merchants of Canada today may be represented in terms of percentages. They are determined by the merchants on their experience of the actual cost of doing business. The same is true all the way up- the jobber, the wholesaler and the retailer. When these people receive an article from the manufacturer, they have to provide a place for selling it, employees, the cost of financing the transaction, bad debts, various social insurances such as workmen's compensation and unemployment insurance-all these things are part of the cost of doing business. Then comes the return on the investment. The actual cost of doing business also depends to some extent on the type of article produced. The member for Moose Jaw could probably give the house excellent examples of the difference in cost when one handles a very small article and a large article.
It made no difference on the articles I handled for the parliamentary assistant.

I want to be the first to thank the member for Moose Jaw for the very low markup he took on the article he handled for me. I believe the hon. member could give a full explanation of all these things which are incorporated in the wholesalers' and retailers' cost of doing business.
Then, as a general rule of thumb, in order to obviate the necessity of making many calculations, the merchant adds a 10, 15, or 20 per cent markup as the cost of doing business. Let us return to the article costing a dollar, which I mentioned yesterday and which the member for Rosetown-Biggar took as a good example because the calculations involved are simple. This article cost a dollar, and after going through the jobber, the wholesaler and the retailer, it resulted in a

100 per cent increase, so that without sales tax the article would cost $2. Formerly, with the addition of the 25 per cent sales tax, the selling price to the consumer would have been $2.50. Those people have said, therefore, that according to their experience the cost of doing business on a one dollar article was $1.
We are now charging 10 per cent at the manufacturers' level. This means that after these three people calculate the cost of doing business, they add this extra 10 per cent. Ten cents in the case of a dollar item does not seem very large. However, when one considers that it is a thousand dollars on ten thousand dollars, and that the carrying charges on such a sum would be an extra charge on the business it begins to loom quite large. A manufacturer should be able to give a price of $1.10, then have the article go through these three stages and reach the consumer at $2.11. Whether it is sold for $2.11 or $2.20 will depend upon competition.
We are now returning to a position of abundant supply. You see evidence of competition every time you pick up your newspaper. Sales are advertised, and we realize that competition is returning. If there is no competition, the merchant may be able to get $2.20 instead of the $2.11 which I have used as an example. However, under our system there is an opportunity for a smart young retailer such as the member for Moose Jaw or the member for Halifax to say: There is a business in which a good profit is to be made, so I am going to enter that business. That is how this markup system functions in our economy.
What is the justification for continuing a tax of 10 per cent on such necessities as are listed under resolution 3(a)-trunks, suitcases, bags, and luggage of all kinds?

Are we to continue discussing item No. 3? We have been discussing it most of the time lately.

speechtext: Shall resolution 2 carry?
Resolution 2 has been carried.
Go ahead.
The parliamentary assistant kindly tells me to go ahead.
On what item are we now?

Resolution 2 has not carried
yet, has it?

No.
The parliamentary assistant has said that I may continue.

On a point of order, are we considering resolution 2 or resolution 3? If we are considering No. 2, the member for Cumberland is out of order. There are many of us who wish to say something about No. 2, and we do not want to be told we are out of order, Mr. Chairman, if you permit the discussion on No. 3 to continue.

The parliamentary assistant's explanation of the sales tax and how it is applied is almost as clear as those radio broadcasts. It would take four or five radio broadcasts to clarify it, but I do not intend that to be any reflection on him.
According to resolution No. 2, you are repealing the purchase tax. Now, the general sales tax is a purchase tax. Most of the people outside of this chamber who read resolution No. 2 and the discussion on it will assume this government is repealing the general sales tax of 8 per cent, because that applies on practically everything one purchases.
The hon. member is completely out of order, of course.
I should like to get these taxes clarified. My impression of what is being done by resolution 2 is that the tax of 25 per cent which applied to certain luxuries during the war is being removed.
That is right.

I believe that none of the taxes which applied to luxury goods during the war should be retained. The way the section is worded makes it misleading. It speaks of the "retail purchase tax", and the sales tax is a retail purchase tax. The sales tax of 8 per cent is applied by the retailer on goods purchased by the consumer. If a person buys lumber, hardware, almost anything else, he is charged the 8 per cent sales tax. I paid it on lumber I purchased less than two months ago. Some of the retailers are honest enough to mark it in as an 8 per cent sales tax, and you know what you are paying.
I suggest to the parliamentary assistant- I know he is new at this job, but perhaps he will learn as he goes along-that his explanation of this retail purchase tax should be clear and precise. Someone should say that the government is removing the 25 per cent luxury tax charged on certain luxury goods during the war, but is applying a 10 per
45781-103J
Excise Tax Act '
cent tax at the manufacturers' level. Then anyone who purchases an article within the field covered by this resolution will under1 stand that no retailer or wholesaler has the right to a markup on the 10 per cent tax. It is being removed completely, and the manufacturer is going to absorb it. None of it can be passed on to the consuming public. Am I right?

The hon. member is wrong in almost everything he has said so far. Resolution 2 very clearly says that the retail purchase tax, which, in order to distinguish it from the federal sales tax, is the legal name by which this tax has been known since it was brought in, is being repealed and will be replaced by an excise tax of 10 per cent. I do not know how much more simply it can be expressed. I do not know how much simpler the English language can be.
As to his second point, on the eight per cent federal sales tax, it was never levied at the retail level. It has always been levied at the manufacturer's level. As to lumber, the eight per cent federal sales tax on lumber was removed at least three if not four years ago. This schedule III which will be on Hansard today-that is schedule III of the present Excise Tax Act-gave a long list of items which in this country today carry no sales tax; that is, no federal sales tax. Foodstuffs and building materials led all the rest of the parade. If the hon. member says that he bought lumber just two weeks ago and paid an eight per cent retail sales tax on it, I would suggest to him that he should see his good friend the hon. member for Lake Centre and institute an action in the matter.

Two months ago. That is just about as clear as was the first statement by the parliamentary assistant. You are repealing the luxury tax of 25 per cent that was imposed during the war and which was handed on to the public.
That is right.
You are repealing that tax and imposing a 10 per cent tax on the manufacturer.
That is right.
That is clear enough. That is exactly what I said in the first place. That is the kind of explanation I want on the record, so that people outside the chamber, in reading it, will understand it.
It is on the record.

It was not on the record before; it is now. That is all I want to find out. I will reserve any questions I have on the general sales tax until we come to item 5.

Excise Tax Act

I agree with the hon. member tor Peterborough West in what he said about this pyramiding of taxes. I do not think there is any member in this committee, regardless of the party to which he belongs, who would suggest that these indirect taxes are not going to pyramid; and naturally, if they start at the manufacturer's level and go through the wholesaler and retailer, they will pyramid a great deal more. As I see this resolution No. 2, although it is not all we should like it to be, it is certainly a great improvement over the law we had before. I certainly do not see why the government cannot collect this tax much more easily and much more efficiently from, say, five or six manufacturers than from
50,000	or 100,000 retailers throughout the country.
Speaking from my own experience, I remember one instance in which we had an indirect tax; there was a tax on pitchers. If it was a pitcher that you put water in, the tax did not apply; but if it was a pitcher that you put on the mantelpiece, you had to pay the tax. I remember that our salesgirls always had a great deal of trouble; it was difficult for them to know when they had to charge tax and when they did not have to charge it. While this resolution is not what we should like it to be, I think it is a great improvement over what we have had.

The hon. member for Halifax can see my correspondence at any time with regard to what I said previously. When he was speaking, he gave the house to understand that he alone was the one who had the 25 per cent luxury tax removed.
No, I did not.
He tried to imply that.
I said that I was one of those who waited on the government. It was a fine delegation.

I might say that the Minister of Finance received thousands and thousands of letters from every part of the country with respect to that tax. That is why it was removed. I waited on the minister not once but many times with regard to that tax. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I say to the hon. member for Halifax that no one today has criticized -the retailers. In my experience I have found only one retailer who was not honest. I do not think it was fair of the hon. member for Halifax to even suggest that anybody criticized the retailers.
Your whole criticism was based on that theme.

I will say this to the hon. member for Halifax, who has criticized us
fMr. Gillis.l
for having given the retailer a markup of 50 per cent. Yesterday as reported at page 1603 of Hansard the parliamentary assistant said:
But mathematically, even though they had, for example, a 50 per cent markup on the $1.10 they would now . . .
And so on. The parliamentary assistant mentioned 50 per cent. The average retailer does charge a 50 per cent markup. Some have to charge more. It depends on whether an article is slow moving and has to be carried in stock for months and months and perhaps years.
Consult any of your grocers.
I am not talking about grocers.
You are talking about retailers.
Because there is not this excise tax on the goods they handle.
You are talking about retailers, though.

I am talking about retailers that are interested in this tax. I am not talking about clothiers either. I agree with the hon. member who preceded me that this tax is better than the 25 per cent tax; but still it is a hidden tax and is one that should be done away with.

I spoke a little while ago about this excise stamp on cigarette boxes. The parliamentary assistant did not say anything about it in reply. Perhaps it was too insignificant for him to bother about. I know that in my speeches I perhaps have a habit of injecting a little bit of levity once in a while, but I do not want any minister of the crown or any parliamentary assistant to think that, because I do that, I am any the less serious in what I say. Sometimes we need to loosen up a little bit in this chamber. Since I called the attention of the parliamentary assistant to this excise stamp, stating that there were twenty cigarettes in this box instead of saying what the tax on those cigarettes was, some public-spirited citizen has sent in to me a little package of matches. I want to compliment the House of Commons for getting these little things out with the crest on them. But there is also printed on the folder: "Excise tax, J cent, paid." I should like to know why that "J cent, paid" is printed on this folder but the amount paid for tax is not printed on the stamp on the cigarette boxes. Why is there that difference?
They are ashamed to put it on.

Either that, or some pressure from somewhere has been exerted to have "20 cigarettes" printed on there instead of the

amount of tax. Will the parliamentary assistant explain why that is there? I am certain that the smoker knows already that there are twenty cigarettes in that package.
At what stage?

Can the parliamentary assistant explain that situation to me? It is not something that is of small value at all. There is a principle involved, and there is some reason why the excise stamp states that there are twenty cigarettes in the package and yet does not state the amount of the tax.

The actual tax on the cigarettes, to which my hon. friend refers, is not an excise tax under this act but an excise duty. The reason that the number of cigarettes is mentioned is this. That tax has been in effect for at least fifty years as on that stamp form. As the tax on cigarettes and tobaccos has varied from budget to budget, if after each budget we had to withdraw all the stamps that were already issued and paid for by the cigarettes and tobacco companies, and bring them back, there would obviously be this extra needless expense at each change in the actual rate. All the stamp shows is that on twenty cigarettes the present excise duty has been paid.
As to the second point, I know he will be glad to know that under resolution No. 6 we are getting rid of that stamp tax on matches and are replacing it with a 10 per cent excise tax. I can answer that question further when we come to resolution No. 6.
I should like to ask one question before we leave this matter. Did I understand the parliamentary assistant to put a schedule on record setting out the articles affected by this tax?

Yesterday afternoon, at the request of the committee, I asked Hansard to put on record schedule III of the Excise Act passed last session, which lists all the articles which are exempt from the payment of either sales or excise tax. It was not given to Hansard but it will be included in today's Hansard. Sections 1, 2 and 6 of our present Excise Act list all the excise taxes. Since most of these are being changed from a variety of rates, 15 per cent, 25 per cent and so on down to 10 per cent, there does not seem to be much point in including that. We should wait for the new bill which will be presented after these resolutions are disposed of, which will have a consolidation of the excise tax rates.

I agree with what the hon. member for Peterborough West said at the beginning of the discussion this afternoon. I do not think his argument has
Excise Tax Act
been answered by the parliamentary assistant who is piloting these resolutions through the committee. I refer to the pyramiding of the costs to the consumer. If an item costs $100 and there is a 10 per cent tax placed on it and a wholesale profit of 25 per cent added and then a retailer's profit of somewhere around 50 per cent, is it not correct, Mr. Chairman, that the consumer then has to pay an extra amount of profit, since percentages are added to the 10 per cent at the beginning? So far as the government is concerned the same result would be arrived at if approximately 6 per cent were put on at the retailer level. On an item costing one dollar it would mean a saving of about 9 cents to the consumer. Why should the consumer have to pay another 9 per cent more than would be necessary to collect the same amount of money for the government?

I tried to explain as best I could what happens on the actual build-up of what is called the markup. The position of the opposition is this. They are not criticizing the retailer. They agree that most retailers are working on a very low margin of profit; that is, dollars and cents profit, because that is the only sort of profit that pays bills, not percentages. Therefore if you say there is pyramiding certainly the government is not getting it. It means the retailer is getting it, and yet the assertion is made that the retailer is working on a low margin. It is obvious, whether the tax is put on at the wholesale or the retail level, the retailer is still going to have that amount of money in percentages, the amount of money necessary to market the goods. That is the argument. It is quite true that if the government levied the sales tax at the retail level instead of the manufacturers' level we could cut the rate in half, if the whole markup was a hundred per cent. The factor which gauges the tax rates that the government has is the amount of revenue we must raise to satisfy the needs of the Dominion of Canada. I have noticed that many hon. members are anxious to have taxes abolished, but I also notice that when the estimates are up for discussion many hon. members are most helpful to the ministers in suggesting bigger expenditures in their particular fields. I have not very much experience in the house of hon. members offering some new tax fields for the government to enter to raise more money, or alternatively where cuts may be made in some of the government departments. In the Department of Finance we are faced with the problem of raising the necessary money, through taxes, to meet the estimates of expenditures of the federal government.

Excise Tax Act

That does not answer the point. To be more explicit, suppose an article costs one dollar and the tax of 10 per cent is not put on in this fashion, and the wholesaler's profit, for argument's sake is the amount that the hon. member for Peterborough West suggested, namely, 25 per cent. That brings the price to $1.25 at that level. The retailer charges 50 per cent markup. That brings the price to $1,875. With a 6 per cent tax at the retail level the government could get more money than it would get with the 10 per cent tax at the manufacturer's level, and the total cost of the article would be $1.97.

Once again, these two factors enter into the picture. The government's tax program is first of all predicated on the amount of money we must raise, and we receive that amount of revenue through the 10 per cent excise tax. The second point is that hon. members on the other side have repeated that they do not think the retailer is taking advantage of it, that he is competitive, and that therefore it is not percentages, it is dollars and cents which are marked up, and which he needs to pay the cost of his business and other costs which he has to encounter. If the tax is levied at the manufacturer's level the cost of obtaining the money from the bank and the extra cost of servicing that money enters into it. Whether the tax is levied at that level or at the retail level he still has the cost of marketing his goods; that is, the jobber, the wholesaler and the retailer. So far as collection is concerned, the hon. member for Moose Jaw pointed out that from his own practical experience, and as the members of the Department of National Revenue can certainly certify, there is a tremendous improvement in that operation and in the cost of collections from a few manufacturers rather than from thousands of retailers across this country.
The consumer is paying for it.
The consumer of course pays for the cost of collection through the general taxes.

What the .parliamentary assistant is trying to do is to make the manufacturer a tax collector for the dominion government. If you want to get away from pyramiding these taxes, put the sales tax and the purchase tax at the retail level, and you will soon get rid of pyramiding and you are also getting more money in that way. And if you do place these taxes at the retail level you will get so much political pressure brought to bear that we will soon be rid of these taxes altogether.

Where will we get the
money?
You will get more from the retailer than you will from the wholesaler.

speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
3.	That the following excise taxes be reduced from 35 per cent to 10 per cent, namely the excise taxes on: (a) trunks, suitcases, bags, and luggage of all kinds; (b) ash trays, tobacco pipes, and smokers' accessories; and (c) fountain pens, propelling pencils, and desk accessories.

In discussing this resolution, what explanation has the parliamentary assistant for the continuation of the excise tax of 10 per cent on necessities such as trunks, bags and luggage of all kinds? Is the ordinary sales tax imposed on these items and the 10 per cent excise tax superimposed? What consideration, if any, is being given to the extra competition of manufacturers of these articles because of the 20 per cent depreciation of sterling? I refer to goods from the sterling area, which are imposing unfair competition on manufacturers to whom I refer. I am pleased indeed that the senior member for Halifax agreed with my statement. He referred to the Christie Trunk and Bag Company in my constituency. They have been carrying on for many years, from small beginnings and have expanded to a considerable extent. They are producing stable commodities and have been able to compete with any like production in Canada. They are having imposed upon them this unfair tax of 10 per cent. I repeat that they are manufacturing a necessity to every person in this house and to every home in Canada.

The hon. member's first question was why this tax is continued at all. I think I have already given the reason. We must secure the revenue necessary. It is quite true that luggage is not a luxury. It is a necessity to many people, but it is not as necessary as housing material and food. They are in the totally exempt class.
The second question was whether the sales tax is imposed. Yes, the sales tax is imposed on all articles carrying the excise tax. The excise tax is an extra tax but it is not superimposed. They are parallel taxes.
The third question was in regard to British competition. These luggage manufacturers have had-and they are the first to admit it- very substantial aid this year, in the reduction of this 35 per cent tax down to 10 per cent. This has given them a 25 per cent margin.
The second point, so far as British competition is concerned, is that to my memory every party in the house has given lip service at least to encouraging British imports and putting them on a more competitive basis. But

the moment a British import is put on a more competitive basis we are then asked from certain quarters for a change in the tariff. Our Canadian manufacturers are getting a 25 per cent benefit because of the cut in the tax, and they should be able to compete with the British. We are giving the British entry, but we have at this time to give the British manufacturers better entry into Canada so we can sell our wheat, lumber and fish.

I object to this tax. As the parliamentary assistant has said, we are in favour of giving all the encouragement we can to importations from Great Britain. But, speaking for myself, and I believe for many members in the House of Commons, that must not be done at the cost of closing Canadian industries which have been in existence in Canada for many years.
This 35 per cent tax was a war tax, and we shall agree it was a necessity. The war tax should now be removed entirely. If the government is going to remove 25 of the 35 per cent tax, what justification is there for continuing the 10 per cent? Why should it not all be removed? If it was a war tax, then I say the time has long since passed when the entire tax should be removed.
With that in mind I am going to offer an amendment-and I am going to ask my hon. friend, the senior member for Halifax, to second it. I have not had the opportunity of seeing him. However he has expressed himself definitely in the house-and I presume this committee is sitting now to review the representations made by the parliamentary assistant to the minister. If our representations mean anything, then surely they mean that we have the right to express ourselves.
On that basis I am going to move:
That section 3 be amended by removing the excise tax on trunks, suit cases, bags and luggage of all kinds, and that subsections (b) and (c) be renumbered (a) and (b).
I have not had the consent of the senior member for Halifax, but-
Ask the junior member, then.

Yes, perhaps the junior member-because they generally work together. His great-grandfather, one of the fathers of confederation, came from my constituency. I am sure he will have some interest in the welfare of the county of Cumberland, where his great-grandfather and his grandfather had such famous careers.

I would refer you, Mr. Chairman, to citation 556 in Beauchesne, which states that a committee has not the right to diminish taxation. The house has the right, provided the house at the time suggests an alternative source of revenue in the amount
Excise Tax Act
of the tax removed. Citation 556 at page 165 of the second edition very clearly sets out that there is no power in the committee to diminish taxation.
According to the parliamentary assistant, we are impotent here. We might as well retire and allow the government in this country to be carried on by order in council. That is what we are reduced to.

The hon. member could vote down the entire resolution, if it does not please him and his party, or alternatively, when we are in the house, with Mr. Speaker in the chair, and considering the bill, he could vote out that particular section.

Notwithstanding what the parliamentary assistant has said, I believe every hon. member in the house is in agreement with the stand I have taken. I would like to see them given the opportunity to express themselves.
No, no.
Well, they are subservient then, Mr. Chairman.
On a point of privilege, the hon. member must withdraw the remark that hon. members sitting to his right are subservient.
I withdraw it if there are some here going to object, but everyone knows what I mean.

I resent very much that remark, and I do not think the hon. member meant to say what he said. I am amazed that an hon. gentleman of his experience should rise in his place and continually suggest that this tax be reduced. He knows very well that we are paying an extra $35 million or $40 million in interest on our increased debt due to the war. When he suggests that we ought to abolish all these taxes surely he has not given the matter sufficient thought.
I have a very high regard for his intelligence. I should like to make it clear that there are manufacturers in my riding who have difficulties to contend with, and they would like to have excise taxes removed. I have never felt however that in a matter of this kind we should speak for any one individual manufacturer.

Mr. Chairman, had the amendment offered by the hon. member for Cumberland been in order I should have had much pleasure in seconding it, for the purpose of striking out subsection (a) of section 3. While this tax is legal, and all that sort of thing, it is not a fair tax upon the consumers

Excise Tax Act
of this country. When the time comes I may attempt to find out from the government how they could strike out subsection (a) and also strike out or amend section 9, where the tax on wine is reduced from 50 cents to 25 cents per gallon. There is a luxury, Mr. Chairman, where I believe the extra tax might be obtained by leaving the excise tax on wine as it is at the present time.
Carried.

As the hon. member for Cumberland for some reason or other has brought my name into this matter-and I am sure that perhaps on the advice of his leader he was well advised in endeavouring to bring me into it-

The amendment reads:
That section 3 be amended by removing the excise tax on trunks, suitcases, bags, and luggage of all kinds, and that subsections (b) and (c) be renumbered (a) and (b).

I repeat my point, that this is clearly out of order. I would refer hon. members to citations 552 and 556 of Beauchesne's second edition, and also May's twelfth edition. I quote the pertinent part of citation 552 as follows:
Amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another tax, of equivalent amount, for that proposed by the government.
If an hon. member moves to reduce the tax revenue, then he must propose a tax that will bring in an equivalent revenue. Obviously the purpose of the rule is to prevent the opposition gleefully moving for the abolition of all taxes. Under the rules they must propose an alternative tax in order to give the government the same revenue.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think citation 552 quoted by the parliamentary assistant is somewhat pertinent to the amendment before the house. As this is an interesting point which has come up for the first time since I have been in the chair, I should like to study it and would suggest that the resolution stand and I will rule upon this matter later on.
That is quite agreeable, but first I should like the parliamentary assistant to tell us what revenue is expected to accrue under paragraph (a).

The previous revenue was approximately $6 million; it is expected there will be a loss of revenue of $4 million; therefore, it is expected that the revenue under this item will be about $2 million.

Resolution 4 agreed to.
5. That the sales tax on the following articles be repealed: lactose; malt syrup except when sold for beverage purposes; diesel powered self-propelled trucks, mounted on rubber tired wheels, for off highway use exclusively at mines and quarries, and complete parts thereof.

I should like to protest against ice cream still being taxable. This is food, it is not a luxury item. This tax is directed at the nickels of the children. I think ice cream is a much more wholesome food for children than gum or candy, the tax on

Excise Tax Act
which has been removed. Ice cream is a by-product of the dairy industry and there is likely to be a surplus in this industry before very long, particularly in view of the increased rents that are to be charged under which people will not have as much money to spend for food. I protest this tax on ice cream and ask the parliamentary assistant to tell the committee what revenue he expects to derive from it and to make some general comments on the situation.

I should like to supplement what has been said by the hon. member for Saskatoon. Ice cream is important as far as the dairy industry is concerned and it has always been classed as a food. It is used as a food in hospitals and by children and it seems to me that this tax is most unfair to the dairy industry which, as all hon. members know, has received some very hard knocks. Margarine is now in competition with butter, which places an added burden on the dairy farmers. I submit that this matter should be considered carefully by the committee.
As far as the farmers of my section of the country are concerned, they depend almost entirely on dairy products for their living. I have received a number of telegrams from the dairy interests in my constituency requesting that this tax be removed and I hope the parliamentary assistant will be able to give us some encouragement in this regard.
This matter has been referred to by many hon. members. As far as dairy products are concerned, milk and butter are classed as staple foods and they are not subject to either sales tax or excise tax.
But not ice cream.

Forty-six per cent of the ice cream sold in Canada is sold in the form of cones. Another large but undetermined percentage is sold in the form of sundaes and dishes of ice cream, and a substantial percentage is sold in the form of bricks for use in the home as a dessert. As the hon. member has said, ice cream is in competition with candies and chocolates and chewing gum. Candy, chocolates and chewing gum used to be subject to a thirty per cent excise tax as well as the eight per cent sales tax. At that time ice cream sold in the form of cones enjoyed the protection of that thirty per cent. That thirty per cent tax has now been removed entirely and all these confections are now on the same level as ice cream, all being subject to the eight per cent sales tax.
I turn now to the comparatively small fraction of the ice cream production that is sold as a food to be used as a dessert. All foodstuffs are not exempt from the eight per
cent sales tax. All staple foodstuffs are exempt from this tax, but desserts such as gelatine preparations commonly used in the Canadian household are not exempt. Therefore ice cream when used as a dessert is on exactly the same footing with these other forms of desserts.
The situation today with regard to ice cream sold in the form of ice cream cones and desserts is that it no longer enjoys the preferential position it used to have in relation to chocolates, pop, candy and chewing gum.

May I move away from a subject of low temperature to one which I think hon. friends will find to be of a somewhat higher temperature, particularly among those who have from time to time discussed the conditions under which the weekly newspapers of Canada operate at the present time. No doubt the parliamentary assistant has before him, or should have before him, the brief of the Canadian Weekly Newspapers Association arising out of their annual meeting at Niagara Falls nearly a year ago, one of the resolutions of which found its way to the desk of the Minister of Finance some time earlier this year. Unfortunately it did not seem to carry as much weight with the minister as one would have expected when he was preparing his budget last spring and again this fall. I think therefore it is only fit and proper that the committee should know the position which the Canadian Weekly Newspapers Association, with its many members across Canada, is facing at the present time with regard to the sales tax on newsprint.
Perhaps I could not do better than to read to the committee parts of the brief because it is short, and one which I think ought to be commended because of its clarity and the convincing arguments that it contains. The members of the Canadian Weekly Newspapers Association, which represents no less than 564 weekly newspapers in Canada, no small number as the parliamentary assistant will readily admit, decided that representations should be made to the federal government requesting that the 8 per cent tax on newsprint should be abolished. The basis for that request is set out in clear and concise fashion. I think the committee and the government would do well to ponder the matter because it seems to me the arguments in favour of their presentation are very powerful. The brief reads in part:
X. The tax does not apply to Canadian or American magazines, circulated in Canada, and competing with weekly newspapers in the national advertising field.
In other words, there is discrimination of a clear character there.

Excise Tax Act
2.	Comic books, certain week-end papers, pulp and fiction magazines printed in Canada (containing advertising) are exempt.
That is also discrimination.
3.	Radio broadcasting facilities, also a powerful competitor in the advertising field, are exempt from this tax.
Still another instance of discrimination.
4.	A survey of prices paid for newsprint by member publishers in various parts of Canada indicates an unjust inequality in the amount of taxes collected on a unit of one ton of newsprint.
5.	In each of the foregoing there is an element of discrimination which this association feels can be eliminated only by exempting newsprint used in the publication of weekly newspapers from this tax.
