It has been put before the minister in a way that I think the government would like to have most briefs presented, concise and factual, and at the same time not in a vein particularly critical of the policy of the government.
I only rise at this time to place their position on the record so that the government may have an opportunity to consider favourably what I think is something that affects a most important section of the Canadian people, the men and women who publish week by week the important news which reaches the eyes of weekly subscribers from one end of Canada to the other.

I should like to return to a subject upon which I started to speak a few moments ago, and that is the portable irrigation sprinkler systems now used extensively on farms in western Canada. When I attempted to raise this subject under section 2, the parliamentary assistant said it was entirely a sales tax that applied to them, but I still believe that is incorrect judging by the amount of tax which was collected. I know that two of these sprinkler systems were purchased by adjoining farmers. The cost was approximately $3,000. On that, they had to pay tariff charges of $300 and taxes of approximately $700, making a total of approximately $1,000 in taxes or tariff charges.
These sprinkler systems will be increasingly used, particularly in any of the dry areas of western Cananda in which water is available either in dugouts, deep wells, streams or such sources of supply. The use of them avoids a lot of the difficulties inherent in the regular irrigation systems. It avoids the necessity of

Excise Tax Act
levelling the land and putting in irrigation ditches. A lot of the land is too hilly for ordinary irrigation systems. By means of this sprinkler system, the water can be taken out of the ditch and put on any of the land that is fit for cultivation.
As I say, these systems have already been used in the last year or two to a considerable extent. In the future, they are likely to be used a great deal. For tariff purposes, excise and sales tax purposes, I believe these sprinkler systems should be considered as farm machinery. Since they have not been used extensively so far, they have not been included in the appropriate item as farm machinery. Instead of that these systems are classified along with pipe, pumps and things of that sort for tariff, excise and sales tax purposes. Some time ago I brought this matter up during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and requested that this type of equipment be considered when the budget resolutions were being drafted. I would ask again that that be done, and that the parliamentary assistant introduce an amendment under the appropriate item removing the tax on this type of equipment.
Looking over schedule III to which the parliamentary assistant referred yesterday, which sets up the materials exempt from sales tax or excise tax, I see items such as baling twine for baling farm produce, drain tiles for agricultural purposes, gopher poison, grain or seed cleaning machines and parts thereof. This type of equipment is going to be much more important so far as increasing the food production of this country is concerned. It will increase the production of grain and will be important to the livestock which is fed on that grain. It certainly seems to me that a change should be made and the tax removed from this equipment.
Although there are no tariff changes mentioned at this time, I believe the tariffs should be amended to admit these sprinkler systems duty free. These systems are not made in Canada now, but I hope they will be soon. It is true that the aluminum pipe which is used is made in Canada to some extent, but the supply has not been sufficient to enable people to equip themselves with it, and as a result most of it comes from the United States. I do hope the parliamentary assistant will make a statement about that.

I should like to associate myself with the hon. member for Calgary East in his request for consideration of these sprinkler systems. One of the P.F.R.A. officials said in Regina some months ago that this new type of irrigation may revolutionize agriculture in western Canada. Not only do I
believe the government should cease to tax it, but I believe the minister should, if at all possible, make it easier for the farmers to obtain that equipment from the United States. As I understand it, today there is more or less of an embargo upon it in order to save United States dollars. This makes it almost impossible to secure that equipment. I should like to give my heartiest support to what the member for Calgary East has said.

I should like to say a word about this matter. Really, it is more important than it may appear to many of the members in the house. Many of the irrigation projects in western Canada, especially those with small dams, make it very difficult to irrigate the land by gravity. If sprinkler systems were obtainable, it would mean that a larger portion of the land could be irrigated.
People who have not lived in the drought areas of western Canada will find it difficult to realize just what it means to a farmer in that area to be able to irrigate a small garden, or a field, to have fodder for his stock. This system might increase the areas that could be successfully irrigated by means of these small projects. I urge the government, therefore, to give serious consideration to trying to make cheaper sprinkling systems available.

While I agree with the representations that have been made by the three previous speakers, it is about another matter that I should like to speak at this time. It is my understanding that, when provincial governments purchase articles which would normally bear this 8 per cent sales tax, the tax is paid by the provincial government but later remitted by the federal government. In my opinion, it is quite proper that one government should not tax another government. What is forgotten, evidently, is that there is a third level of government in Canada, namely the municipal government.
The municipal government, within its sphere of activity, is much more important to the Canadian people than any other level of government. In fact, this government is closer to the people and affects their daily activities to a greater extent. While provincial governments enjoy the remission of sales tax on commodities which are not to be resold, the municipality is not in the same position. Today, municipalities are building better roads, which necessitates the use of modern, heavy equipment. This equipment is costing a tremendous amount of money, and the sales tax, being based on the cost, is also running very high. My personal view is that it would be extremely difficult to advance a sound argument against extending to the municipalities the same consideration that is

Excise Tax Act
now extended to the provincial government, namely, the remission of the sales tax on equipment which must necessarily be bought and used in connection with their operations on the roads.
I urge upon the parliamentary assistant that he impress upon the minister the necessity of giving this matter early and serious consideration. I might add that these municipalities are penalized in a second way in that this road-building equipment is classed as industrial equipment for tariff purposes. I intended to bring that up when we were considering tariffs. I would urge the parliamentary assistant not to let this matter die because it is of extreme importance. It would eliminate a degree of discrimination between one level of government in Canada and another.

1 should like to support the plea that has been made by the member for Red Deer. I may say that at the last session I brought the same difficulty to light, but was not successful in having the requests of two or three town councils in my constituency granted. Since the member for Red Deer has brought up the question, I should like to support the appeal he has made. As to the case that was made by the hon. member for Calgary East, supported by the hon. member for Moose Jaw and the hon. member for Melville, I also want to express my hope that the government will do something in that regard. As they have pointed out, up to the present time we have not enjoyed many of the benefits of irrigation, and for that reason have not needed the irrigation systems that have been spoken of. In the interests of Canadian agriculture and Canadian consumers as a whole, I believe the government would do well to grant the request made by those hon. members.

The observations made by the hon. members will be carefully considered by the government. The reason why they may not have been included up to now may be the one pointed out by the hon. member for Calgary East, that this is a new type of irrigation; although I recall seeing some of these sprinkler systems in the Okanagan valley in British Columbia. The schedule gives considerable concessions to farm equipment. I do not doubt that the representations of the hon. members will be carefully considered, and I am quite sure that the Minister of Agriculture will add his word to those already spoken.

On behalf of those in the north, in the areas that are just coming under cultivation, I wish to say a few words with regard to this big machinery for municipalities. This big machinery is something that the individual cannot very well take hold

of. The municipalities are taking hold of this machinery and are clearing land and putting it under cultivation. When they buy this machinery worth from $9,000 up to $30,000 they have to pay the 8 per cent because the municipality buys it. I should like to see that sales tax taken off that machinery just as the sales tax is taken off farm machinery because it is for farm work.

I should like to thank the parliamentary assistant for his remarks and for saying that the government will give consideration to removing the sales tax or whatever taxes there are-I think there are some excise taxes also-and the tariffs on this sprinkler irrigation equipment. I do not see, however, why there need be any delay in doing that. I should like to request that, before we finish with these resolutions, some consideration be given to the matter and that if at all possible the tax concession be brought in at this session. Before we get around to passing resolutions in the next session of parliament, there will probably be people who will have to be buying these things. It will possibly be well on in the spring or summer before we are back at this sort of business and when there will be any further opportunity to put into effect these tax concessions. As I say, it is likely to be too late for a considerable number of people. In many cases it would mean that the price of this equipment would be beyond their means and they would not be able to buy it whereas, if this tax were off, they would be able to do so. As I indicated in this one case, the tax and tariff combined amounted to more than 25 per cent of the total cost. That would mean that some people will not be able to buy this equipment and as a result would lose crops which they might otherwise save. Therefore I think it is urgent that consideration should be given to this matter at this session, and that these concessions should be made at this session, in the interests of dry-land farming and also in the interests of food production.

I understand that gasoline shovels are not manufactured in Canada. In our part of the country they are an essential implement in the building of roads and for the general development of the country. If these machines are not made in Canada, it seems unfair that a tariff should be levied on those that are brought in from outside. I understand that there is one factory in Canada which produces a certain gasoline shovel, but that it is not suitable for the work in our particular part of the country. Therefore a greatly added cost is placed upon road building and the development of the country.

Excise Tax Act
Are hospitals, when they advantage with regard to diesel-powered make purchases, at present exempted from trucks and that now we are just adding mines sales tax?	and quarries to the schedule?
Hospitals which are approved by the various provincial governments are exempted.

That brings me to one point to which I should like to draw the minister's attention. In my constituency we have an old age home, in which there are about fifty people who ordinarily would be in the hospital owing to the fact that their health is so bad. But there is no room for them in the hospital. Therefore they have to be put in this home for the aged. The sisters there are having great financial difficulties in keeping those people there. They are obliged to make major purchases from time to time. Just recently they had to purchase an elevator in order to move these old age pensioners from the third floor down to the first floor; that elevator cost them $1,200 and they had to pay sales tax on it. On all their purchases they are having to pay this sales tax.
The point I should like to make is this. If the government is exempting hospitals from this sales tax, would it not be possible also to exempt from it institutions such as orphanages, homes for the aged and the like? Perhaps it is not feasible to do so, but it seems reasonable to me that, when they make a request of that kind, it should be considered; and I should greatly appreciate receiving an answer from the parliamentary assistant.

I can assure the hon. member that careful consideration has been given to the matter. One reason why careful consideration has been given to it is that the minister himself has in the heart of his own riding one of the largest of these homes for the aged. The difficulty, of course, comes in drawing the line. There is no difficulty with regard to hospitals because they are certified as hospitals by the various provincial governments. But as to the institutions referred to, it is difficult to know where to draw the line between convalescent homes, nursing homes, orphanages, homes for old age pensioners and the like. At the moment it has been possible to give this concession only to hospitals. It was not given in this budget but rather in a previous one. I can assure the hon. member that active consideration is being given to the next groups; that is, those groups of charitable institutions.
I see that the sales tax is being repealed on diesel-powered trucks for use off the highway, if they are used at mines and quarries. Do I understand that the logging industry already enjoys this
It has been extended to mines and quarries if the trucks are not used on the public highway.
The logging industry already enjoys it.

I should like to bring the discussion back for one more moment to the subject which I had broached; that was the taxation on ice cream. The parliamentary assistant's reply was perhaps more ingenious than logical, and he omitted to answer the one question which I asked, namely, what revenue the tax on that particular commodity brought in. I do not know what he is going to tell me; but whatever it is, I do not think it will be justified having regard to the hardship that it will create for the children who buy the ice cream and for the dairy people around my city, for instance. A great many farmers in my constituency make their living, as a matter of fact, from the delivery of milk to the various dairies in Saskatoon, where the commodity is turned into ice cream and then shipped out. It is an important industry not only to the children in the community but to many of their parents as well. I hope the parliamentary assistant will give me that information.

Before the minister replies, I should like to say a word on this matter. According to all the reports we read in the press today, we are accumulating larger and larger surpluses of dairy products. Just yesterday in the local papers it was reported that some 73 million pounds of butter was being held in cold storage. We have large quantities of powdered and condensed milk and some 14 million pounds of cheese. Ice cream is an outlet for some of our dairy products which are accumulating in cold storage today. The government should give serious consideration to trying to provide a home market because we have lost our British market for powdered and condensed milk and many other dairy products. Surely we should be building up our home market.
To bring this thing to a head I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon:
That section 5 be amended to add ice cream to the articles on which sales tax is removed and that an amount of sales tax be added to the present sales tax on wines and spirituous liquors that will equal any revenue loss to the government as a result of this amendment.
I believe it is necessary to provide some other revenue that will equal the loss of any revenue which the government may sustain.

Excise Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, I suggest that this amendment is out of order for the same reason that the last one was. In my view an hon. member cannot just make a blanket suggestion that we increase the tax on wines and spirituous liquors. He will have to make a specific recommendation for an increase in the form of this resolution, an increase of so much on wine, so much on tobacco and so much on spirits. If he puts it in that form I am sure he will be in order.
Mr. Cold well: What is the citation?

Under resolution 9, what gallonage of wine is taxed and what revenue is produced? The resolution reads:

Mr. Chairman, I should like to
concur in many of the things that have been said by hon. members who have spoken on the repeal of the sales tax on heavy machinery used by the rural municipalities. The municipalities in western Canada have been using these big machines not only for breaking land and constructing roads but also to construct dugouts and small stock-watering dams for individual farmers. By so doing we are endeavouring to get them away from strictly grain growing and into more diversified farming. That is something that the Saskatchewan association of rural municipalities have asked for, for a good many years. I hope that the government will give due consideration to the repeal of this tax on heavy machinery.

At this point I should like to make an appeal for consideration to be given, in next year's budget, to the repeal of the sales tax on medical equipment. I appreciate that resolutions, once prepared and introduced in the house, are rarely if ever changed in the year of their introduction. Therefore I would direct my remarks in support of a request that this matter be given most earnest consideration to see if it cannot be contained in next year's budget. I have here a bulky file which comes from a gentleman who suffers from cancer. He uses equipment which can only be imported from the United States. It is specialized equipment and is made only in that country. Not only is a duty charged on that equipment but there is in addition the 8 per cent sales tax on top of the price, plus the duty. He has given me a sample of the way in which it works out. He had to buy specially made surgical dressings. The retail price was $11. The duty of 20 per cent added $2.20, making the price $13.20. On top of that was charged a sales tax of 8 per cent, not on the purchase

Excise Tax Act
price of $11, but on the purchase price, plus duty, of $13.20. The sales tax came to $1.06. Therefore the total price was $14.26 instead of $11. I suppose it is difficult to draw a distinction between medical equipment which must be used in serious cases and medical equipment on which it might be said it was proper to charge some form of revenue tax. I feel it is not a job beyond the potentialities of this department. Certainly people who are suffering from serious diseases such as cancer should not have to pay sales tax on the purchase of equipment without the use of which they could not exist.
Hon. members know what happens when cancer affects internal organs. In order to get about at all the sufferer has to have these expensive and complicated appliances. He virtually has to have them in order to go on living, and it seems to me that type of equipment should not be subject to sales tax.
While I am speaking about sales tax I would go further and ask that consideration be given in next year's budget to changing the tariff structure so that similar items which have to be imported from the United States, because they are not made in Canada, might not be subject to duty. I have had correspondence with the Department of National Revenue in the matter, and it is agreed that the type of equipment I have in mind is not made in Canada and can be secured only from the United States. As I have pointed out, it is subject to a tariff charge of 20 per cent.
In my correspondence with the Department of National Revenue it is pointed out by them that the tariff regulations now make it imperative that they charge the duty, that there is no alternative, and that the only way the situation can be adjusted is by a change in the tariff regulations through the budget resolutions. As no such action is contemplated in this year's budget, it is not open to me to move a resolution because there is no heading under which I could do so. I do take this opportunity however to urge the most sympathetic consideration of the plight of these people who have to obtain expensive medical appliances from the United States, without which they virtually could not live. I urge that this and similar types of equipment be relieved from duty and sales tax. Would the parliamentary assistant give us at least the undertaking that the matter will be seriously considered before the next budget is brought down.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether the hon. member for Kamloops was just unfortunate in the item he chose to exemplify his point in his argument. However, I presume he is referring to a colostomy pad, an absorption pad used for a certain
type of patient suffering from cancer of the lower bowel. I am sure there is no necessity of going to the United States to procure an absorption pad. There may be some other items the hon. member has in mind and to which he has not referred; but I do not think it is wise to rise in one's place and suggest the removal of duty from articles just because someone fancies that he receives a better article in the United States.
Let me give an example in this connection. I was called out on a very stormy day during the winter to see a patient who, it was reported, was very ill. I drove all day in a blizzard, and was stuck many times so that I had to get farm teams to pull me out. Finally I arrived, to find that the man had arthritis deformans. He was crippled, and lying in bed, but in addition he was dying from cancer of the larynx.
I advised them that the only thing they could do was to keep the poor patient comfortable under a sedative which his physician had already prescribed. However, I had no sooner left than an insurance salesman came along and said, "You should not have called that fellow in. My advice is much better. I had an uncle down in Iowa in just the same condition this man is in, and we got him an electric suit. Get one of those."
Those people were too poor to pay for my trip, but somehow or other they procured an electric suit at a cost of $125, upon which duty, taxes and everything else had to be paid. They put that poor patient in the electric suit-boots, hood and all-only to find that there was no electricity on the farm to plug it into.
I would submit that some of the suggestions we have heard today have been given just as much thought as was given to the condition of that patient and to the equipment for his treatment.

With the details of the hon. member's medical practice I am of course not familiar; but I rather fancy that upon reflection he would not wish it to be understood, from any remarks he has made, that he has no sympathy for those in this country who, because no suitable apparatus is manufactured in Canada, are compelled to rely upon articles imported from the United States. I am sure he did not wish hon. members to draw that inference from his remarks. I am sure that one in his position, with his knowledge of the suffering of some of these people whose lives could be made more comfortable by the use of appliances made only in the United States, would support the request I had made-which was not for a general and sweeping removal of the tariff items on all articles, whether they are

Excise Tax Act
made in Canada or not, but was confined to the removal of tariff items on these surgical and other appliances which must be worn by sufferers from cancer, and which are not made in this country.
Correspondence I have received is to the effect that this particular type of equipment is not made in Canada, and in this particular case it is the only type which would bring relief to the sufferer.

Mr. Chairman, may I correct any false impression I may have left. I do not think I gave the impression that I was unsympathetic to sufferers. I am sure my young friend, who was with me overseas, knows that I am sympathetic to those who suffer, and that I looked after them to the best of my ability.
I think he also knows that the item he has cited is an unfortunate one, because it can easily be obtained in this country,- I will add that the treatment of cancer is just as advanced in this country as anywhere else, and that those who suffer from cancer are not being neglected. I want that clearly understood. We have in my city of Regina the most advanced cancer clinic on this continent, and the people there are not suffering from neglect.
If the hon. member would take the trouble to consult physicians and hospitals to find out from them what items would make the lives of these people easier, I would be the first to second a motion to have duty on such items removed. But I resent the implication that I am not sympathetic to the suffering.
The Depuiy Chairman: May I express the hope that from now on the discussion may be more relevant to the resolution before the committee.

The hon. member for Calgary East pointed out that certain equipment was necessary for purposes of irrigation in western Canada. My understanding was that this equipment might almost revolutionize agriculture. We spend large sums of money to subsidize western agriculture. The hon. member suggested that there was a shortage of this equipment which appears to be composed of aluminum pipe. We have in this country one of the greatest aluminum industries on the North American continent.
Inasmuch as this is a new field, and the manufacturing of this requirement would pave the way for a new industry, does the parliamentary assistant not feel that the government would effect a large saving in subsidies paid to agriculture by developing an industry of this kind which could meet these requirements in Canada? Instead of sending our raw aluminum to the United States where it is used for their purposes,

with a dribble coming back here as they see fit, an industry should be established in this country to use our own raw materials. If that were done it would eliminate all this question of tariffs and taxes. Would the parliamentary assistant comment on that?

I do not think that this matter comes under the Department of Finance, but I am quite sure that if this new equipment, which apparently is being used so successfully in western Canada, reaches any real volume of sales it will not be very long before the industrialists of eastern Canada will be using Canadian aluminum to satisfy the demand. That is perhaps the only argument we have for the retention of such an item.

I do not believe the parliamentary assistant commented on the matter, which I raised a moment ago, of sales tax on heavy equipment used by municipalities. This is a rather important matter in western Canada where many of the municipalities are receiving grants under the P.F.R.A. to assist in the digging of dugouts, since they find that they require such equipment. Does the parliamentary assistant know whether the sales tax is rebated to the municipalities who buy this heavy equipment when it is used for P.F.R.A. purposes? A rebate is made to the provincial governments when they purchase this type of equipment and I should like to know if the municipalities receive a similar rebate.

The exemption of sales tax to the province is made to the crown in the right of the province. What is being asked now is a further concession to the provinces to be passed on to the municipalities, or perhaps a concession direct to the municipalities. At the present time no such concession is being granted in this budget. As far as any tariff changes are concerned, they would be considered when the tariff act is under discussion.

I should like to go back to this matter of sales tax on surgical equipment. I am glad the hon. member for Regina City stated that there were no implications in his remarks such as I suggested there might have been.
There was no implication in my remarks that I was not sympathetic to the patient and I want to ask the hon. member-
Sit down.

There seems to be some conflict of opinion as to whether or not this equipment to which I referred was obtainable in Canada. Unfortunately I do not know anything about medical equipment, but my correspondent goes on to say:
The apparatus which I have to use is, to the best of my knowledge, all manufactured in the States, and is all patented. The result is that I not only have to pay a very high price for it but must pay duty and sales tax as well.

It is in accordance with that suggestion that I am making these representations. I submit that where an item can only be secured from outside Canada it should not be subject to duty or sales tax.

In the past the government has shown considerable sympathy toward the problem raised by the hon. member and I would refer him to items 476 to 480a of the tariff act which cover a great number of surgical and medical supplies which can be imported free of duty from the United States. Then there is a section in the Excise Act which exempts similar surgical and medical supplies from the sales tax. Then there are the further exemptions of sales tax on articles purchased for use in hospitals. As far as purchases by individuals are concerned, I think the hon. member will appreciate the difficulty there would be in deciding just what type of equipment should receive consideration. Would the item "diesel
powered, self-propelled trucks" cover caterpillars?

This resolution applies to diesel powered self-propelled trucks, mounted on rubber tired wheels for off highway use exclusively at mines and quarries. I have never seen an ordinary mine truck equipped with rubber tires. This applies to the diesel trucks used in open mines and quarries.
I am referring to the caterpillar equipment that is used by municipalities for farm work.
That is exempted already under another item in the schedule which I have placed on Hansard. This is a new resolution extending the exemptions to the equipment used in mines and quarries.
By municipalities or farmers?
The answer is no.

We want this equipment
exempted because the municipalities use it just the same as though it were used on a farm and they must pay the 8 per cent. Municipalities in northern Ontario, northern Saskatchewan, northern Manitoba and northern Alberta are breaking up thousands and thousands of acres of land with caterpillar trucks that never go off the land. That equipment wears out on the land and yet the municipalities must pay the 8 per cent sales tax. If you are going to take this off for the miner, it should be taken off for the farmer or the municipality.

If the equipment is for
exclusive farm use it would be exempt under schedule III, but if the municipality uses the equipment for road building or other purposes, it is not exempt. The engine section of schedule III says that such tractors when used exclusively for farming are exempt.

Mr. Chairman, because it is for a municipality they say we must pay on that machinery. That is the reason they will not allow us that deduction. We use it solely on the farm. The scrub cutter never goes off the farm, but it comes from the United States and we have to pay the 8 per cent sales tax on it. It cannot go on a road. It cannot be used anywhere else except on a farm. Because we are a municipality we have to pay that, and we should not have to pay it any more than the dominion government pays it.

Excise Tax Act

The only answer I can give is the answer I have already given. If such equipment is used exclusively on a farm, irrespective of whether the owner is a farmer, municipality or corporation, it is exempt from sales tax.
No, not for a corporation.

I believe we should have the matter cleared up. The parliamentary assistant to the minister asserts that on purchases for municipalities for use on farms the sales tax does not apply, but I can assure him that is not correct. If it is purchased by a municipality they pay the 8 per cent sales tax no matter what it is used for. What I am asking, what the hon. member who brought up the question is asking, and what hon. members in general are asking, is that the government take into consideration the removal of this tax, or at least that the municipality pay the tax and then have it remitted to it. That is now done for the provincial government. May I add that municipalities in my province, and I presume this is true of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and other provinces, are today taking over much of the work formerly done by the provincial government. That is a further reason why consideration should be extended to municipalities.

I should like to have some clarification of resolution No. 7 which has to do with computing the income for 1948 and subsequent taxation years for a member of the clergy or a religious order. I have received an inquiry from a minister of the United Church about this matter, and perhaps the parliamentary assistant could answer it. He asks whether it is the intention of the Minister of Finance that any ordained clergyman, irrespective of his duties in the church or outside the church, shall enjoy this exemption from taxation. In other words, do the words "a regular minister" mean any ordained minister or a minister in a charge? Some ministers are not in a charge, and that is one point this man raised.
There is another point I should like to raise. Provision is made for deduction of the value of the residence provided for the minister or rented by the minister, but what about a house that the minister owns? In many cities, ministers serving congregations own their own houses. This man suggests that such exemptions should be enlarged to include such cases.

The answer to the first question is that it is not necessary for the minister to have what is ordinarily referred to as a charge. He may be assisting a minister or doing general work, but so long as his fulltime occupation is the ministry, then he is allowed this deduction. So far as the second

point is concerned, a minister who owns his own home is allowed the equivalent of the rent he would have to pay if he were renting a house of that type.

If a minister is in some work such as teaching in a college, or something which has to do with the religious denomination to which he is attached, does he come under the provisions the parliamentary assistant has just mentioned?
If, for example, he were secretary to a church council-is that what the hon. member is talking about? It would be full-time religious work, but not necessarily in charge of a congregation.
I am thinking more particularly of a man who is teaching at the United Church college, who is a minister but is not engaged in ordinary ministerial work at the moment.
He would be regarded as a teacher rather than as a minister attending to full-time religious activities.

Mr. Chairman, on this specific question of exemptions for the clergy, I feel that these men who make a complete sacrifice of their entire lives should be taken from the income tax rolls entirely. They should not be taxed in any way, shape, or form. This brings up the question, however, of exemptions that are made for specific purposes. It is my contention that once a person falls within the income tax field, as I attempted to point out the other day, no exemptions whatever should be made because of his particular occupation or profession.
I feel that possibly my remarks on that subject were misconstrued the other day. Once we start making exemptions for any specific purpose, then we open up a vast field which would lead to difficulties in calculation that would render it almost impossible for the income tax department to carry out its function. Suppose exemptions were to be made, to cite a specific case, for professional fees or union dues. I might say that I have been in the labour movement for some time, and as a result of that I learned one very important principle; that no matter how much I differed with the principles that were involved in a particular matter, loyalty meant a great deal in obtaining things which I sought. Possibly that is something a good many of the members here have not had the opportunity of experiencing since they were not in the same happy position as I was.
I feel there should be no particular exemption made for a house or small expenses which may be incurred by members of the

clergy, but my belief is these men should be removed entirely from the income tax roll.

Mr. Chairman, the members at this end could not hear whether or not you were passing certain items. There was quite a bit of noise. Would the minister answer a question relating to resolution No. 3, in regard to dividends which are in an estate. Do those dividends lose their identity?

Under resolution No. 5, I think the minister might very well tell us where all this income tax comes from. It comes largely under resolution No. 5. With respect to this matter of assessment, I would point out that it has a definite bearing on the matter of interest penalties. Income Tax Act

I am sorry if I am contravening the rules, but I think this is a point that is deserving of some consideration by the department. There is a feeling among the taxpayers, and I think it is fairly general, that the government regards this question of interest as a sort of one-way street in its favour. If anybody overpays his taxes, the government conveniently forgets that it has had the use of the taxpayer's money for a year or so, as the case may be. On the other hand, if the taxpayer happens to underestimate his taxes, or happens to make some mistake in his return and is obliged to pay more, then of course the government comes along and exacts the full rate of interest from him. That in itself is bad enough. But there is another point which ought to be stressed. It may be that now the situation is being cured; I think perhaps to a large extent it may be. In the past, the department has been years behind in its assessments. That was not the taxpayer's fault; it was the government's fault. The result was that, because of the arrears of assessments and because of the fact that the government department itself had defaulted in bringing the assessments up to date, and which they should have brought up to date, taxpayers found that they had sometimes perhaps three years' interest to pay-I am not sure whether they went any further- which mounted up to quite a bit of money. Taxpayers complained about that, but so far as I know there never was any redress. The government ought not to put itself in a preferred position to those who have to pay the taxes. After all, if the taxpayer has to pay interest on the money that he owes to the government after the assessment has been made, then if he overpays he ought to be allowed interest on that overpayment. In addition, he should not be penalized because of the default of somebody in the department. Some explanation of the policy of the department ought to be given.

I can tell the hon. member for Peel that if the return of the taxpayer is accurate, which after all is the responsibility of the taxpayer, there is no overpayment or underpayment.
As far as underpayment is concerned, the interest charged is not only interest charged on money which is owing the government but also a penalty to encourage accurate returns of income tax. So far as the other matter is concerned, the hon. member will recall that last year legislation was passed allowing interest at the rate of two per cent on overpayment; but there again overpayment, so far as the taxpayer is concerned, is because-
IThe Deputy Chairman.]
Is that what the taxpayer in default is charged?

So far as the taxpayer in default is concerned it is not only a matter of interest on the money owed to the government but also a penalty to encourage in the first place accurate returns of the taxpayer's income.
May I suggest to the parliamentary assistant that there ought to be some kind of penalty to encourage the government to bring their assessments up to date.

As I recall, the hon. member and his party have been the ones who in past years have urged great reductions in the civil service. The reason we got so far behind during the war was the lack of staff because we were holding down the civil service. We were twenty months behind. By April of next year the assessments will all be up to date. That is why we are able to close the gap from first of all no limit, then to twenty months and now to twelve months in this resolution.
That does not help the man who has had to pay.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: We will revert to resolution 7.

Mr. Chairman, this tax should be wiped off the slate not because ministers do not receive as large a salary as members of parliament but because they have calls that no member of parliament has to answer. I can give an illustration of some of the calls a minister has to make. Suppose he is downtown on a Saturday and sees an old friend whose legs do not seem to be able to carry him very well. He takes him home and puts him in the spare room and keeps him there a day, two days or a week and sobers him up with black coffee. The income tax department will not permit him to take that gift off his income tax. The department does not allow a minister any credit for gifts that he makes which other people do not make. The minister has continual calls on him. They are not made once in a while, but practically every day or at least every week. Because of these gifts I think this tax should be wiped off the slate. I am not speaking of one denomination only. It applies to anybody in religious work. A clergyman has those calls, and he is expected to practise what he preaches, feed the hungry and clothe the naked.

I asked the predecessor of the present minister a question with regard to this particular resolution. I refer to the late minister who is now a judge in Nova Scotia. I asked him this question: Do all the clergy of the Christian churches pay income tax? His

reply was that so far as he knew they did. I am glad that resolution 7 has been amended because clergymen have a great many important duties to perform. They should be all treated alike in this country. The Christian churches should not take precedence over the state. The state has to raise money by this method of income tax to enable the country to pay its debt. Some allowance should be made for all clergy of the Christian church and of other churches who are not of the Christian faith. There is this to be said about the clergy. During the depression and during the period of the late war the clergyman had to be judge, doctor and almost everything. I remember three or four clergymen coming one day to the bar of the house to visit. A few years ago I addressed a bartender's union. Because I was the head of a big city I had to treat them all alike. I said that a lawyer pleads from inside the bar. Today a minister has to use his car. He has to pay for the gasoline. He does not own a house. He has to go down to the police court to help his parishioners out.
In the Toronto district the scale of fines under this whole Income Tax Act, and particularly under this resolution, are heavier than they are in any other court in the country. They are almost five to one. This resolution should be liberally interpreted to include all the Christian clergy. There is one church that does a great deal of good work. I refer to a faith to which I do not belong. I know a great many of the clergy from their seminaries and others, and they do valuable work. That could be applied also to the other Christian denominations. In view of what the clergy are doing to help the people there should be a liberal interpretation of this resolution.

I wish to say a few words on this resolution. We did not know it before in the province of Newfoundland, that is why I draw it particularly to the attention of the parliamentary assistant. Would it not be fairer to tax the minister on gifts or on, shall we say, a private income apart from the return on his direct ministerial duties, or else raise the exemption a little higher for clergymen alone? I presume this applies equally to all provinces but the clergymen in a number of districts in the province of Newfoundland are going to find this a real hardship. I submit that to exempt the direct earnings from the ministerial duties of a clergyman would be the fairer way, or to raise the exemption to $2,000 to $2,500 in this particular case.

First of all I would point out to the hon. member, as was indicated by the hon. member for Kootenay East, that it is
Income Tax Act
difficult when one gets into this business of giving special exemptions to different groups. The present exemption can be justified in that a minister's home is, if I may use the expression, more or less his place of doing business, the place where during week days he ministers to his congregation and performs other functions in connection with his office.
This concession is an improvement in the taxation regulations, as applied to clergymen. There is one point, of course, that because of the incomes which most clergymen receive, a considerable number of them, especially if they are married with children, are now in the exempt class by reason of the increase in the basic deduction in respect of all taxpayers.

I should like to say a word in respect of a further deduction which in my view clergymen should have. A complaint was registered with me about a year ago where it was pointed out that clergymen are not exempt for certain travelling expenses incurred in the discharge of their regular pastoral duties. There are some clergymen occupying charges in western Canada who must cover a considerable area of ground and have considerable travelling to do in that connection. Some even have several churches in different communities to which they must travel once or twice a week. Sometimes they have to travel long distances to conduct funerals for which, on occasion, they do not accept fees. I do not think that as a rule clergymen take fees for conducting funerals. Then there are a number of other reasons for travelling.
Some may have their own cars. In the case brought to my attention neither depreciation on the car nor the gasoline bill was taken into consideration. Most clergymen do not receive large salaries. It is all very well to say that they do not come within the income tax bracket-and we know that many of them do not. But those who do are not allowed travelling expenses. I do suggest to the parliamentary assistant that some consideration should be given to this matter.

Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary assistant indicated a moment ago that it was difficult to set aside any particular occupation or profession for special consideration in the income tax structure. I fancy most members of the committee will agree with that general principle; because it is a national levy and for that reason one would expect the government at least in a general way to take that stand.
I think however that the parliamentary assistant would agree with hon. members who have spoken, that, after all, our ministry, our clergymen, regardless of the denominations

Income Tax Act
to which they belong, make a great contribution to our national life for which compensation is never made in dollars and cents. Perhaps it is never intended that it should be, in the minister's mind-and very often, unfortunately, it is not in the congregation's mind either. I am inclined to think that our clergymen are in an entirely different position because, in a sense, they are in a class in which they render a service, rather than in a money-making class from the income of which is siphoned off a certain percentage.
As has been mentioned by one of my colleagues, clergymen's incomes are derived in different ways. It seems to me the government should give careful consideration to the pleas which have been made on behalf of the clergy in Canada. I do not think many taxpayers would find fault with or be even mildly critical of the government if our clergymen were taken right out of the income tax brackets altogether. There would be some technical objections from the department, but I believe the policy is one which would commend itself generally, because it would be an indication of just how this parliament and the people of Canada judge, appreciate and value the work of this important section of our population which ministers to our people. It would be the most practical way of saying a word of praise to them.
We would not have a nation worth the name if we did not have our churches. For that reason, what I have said should be a guiding factor and an important feature in the formulation of government policy. I know the clergymen would not ask for it, as I am now asking; but it seems to me it is the duty of laymen throughout Canada to speak on their behalf. After all, I believe the laymen of Canada would regard it as a privilege and an honour to bear any extra burden of taxation which would become necessary by exempting these men who render such signal service in the religious life of our nation.

I am not quite clear concerning this resolution. As I understand the hon. member for Peel, the legal profession receives exemptions for expenses; is that correct in respect of people who contribute so little to the welfare of Canada? Am I to understand that the ministerial group, of which I am sure my young friend from Coast-Capilano knows so much, are being taxed? If that is so, then I say through you, Mr. Chairman, and through my young friend to the Minister of Finance, that it is high time they changed their policy.

8.	That, for the 1949 and subsequent taxation years, the exemption from income of an individual in respect of a spouse supported by him shall not be reduced because of exempt income of the spouse.
Would the parliamentary assistant explain this resolution, and tell the committee whether it arises as the result of a court judgment?

I cannot say whether it arises as the result of a court judgment, but it does arise because of the need of one special group. Under the present terms of the Income Tax Act an individual is required to reduce his present exemption by the amount of income of his spouse in excess of $250. In calculating the amount of the spouse's income to be taken into consideration, the law now requires that receipts by her which are not in themselves taxable must be included. The most typical case is probably a wife supporting a husband who was a veteran in receipt of disability pension. Such pensions are not in themselves taxable but at the present time must be taken into consideration in the wife's income, and therefore they become taxable. That is the purpose of the resolution, and the class to which this resolution is intended to refer.
It would include a wife's income as well from any source.
Yes, from any source.

9.	That, for the 1949 and subsequent taxation years, all amounts whether in the form of lump sums or otherwise, received by employees from their employers, whether before, during or after their employment, shall be included in computing income of the employee unless it is established that they cannot reasonably be regarded as consideration for entry into the employment, remuneration for services or consideration for restrictions on the activities of the employee.

Would the
parliamentary assistant explain this in language so simple that even I can understand it?

The purpose of this measure is to defeat practices resorted to by some taxpayers to avoid payment of income tax. These arrangements when found are usually between an employer and an employee of executive rank. In essence, they attempt to convert into a capital payment made in return for certain undertakings given by the employee a payment or series of payments that would otherwise be income of the employee. If such payments wear the guise of a capital payment they may escape income tax. It is only in very exceptional circumstances, however, that a payment made by an employer to an employee is not simply part of the terms of the employment, and it is only fair to the

great majority of taxpayers that they be kept under close surveillance and governed by the most rigid restrictions.
The purpose of the amendment that will be based on this paragraph is to bring all such payments, whether paid in a lump sum or otherwise, under scrutiny by the tax authorities. In the first instance they will all be deemed taxable unless the taxpayer can prove they were not of the type of payment I have mentioned.

I am grateful to the parliamentary assistant for that clear and lucid explanation in simple language, but would he mind telling me what it is all about? What is the evil you are seeking to correct? For instance the last three lines read:
-unless it is established that they cannot reasonably be regarded as consideration for entry into the employment, remuneration for services or consideration for restrictions on the activities of the employee.
I have read that over to myself half a dozen times and I am utterly unable to perceive any sense at all in it. I do not know what it means. Does it mean the payments that might be made to a hockey or baseball player where so much is paid for signing up?
It does.

Then I need not wear the dunce's cap any longer. I think I am the only person in the committee apart from the parliamentary assistant who knew that. We have that one thing explained. Then the resolution goes on:
-remuneration for services or consideration for restrictions on the activities of the employee.
Would that be for a woman who would go out for coffee in the morning at ten o'clock or for tea in the afternoon? What does it mean?

I gave the departmental
explanation; now I shall give my own. A great many attempts have been made in the United States and a few in this country by high executives of companies to get around the special rates of income tax which we have on high salaries by obtaining from the company a lump sum and hedging it around with some qualification in order to make it look like a capital gain rather than a payment for past services or present services or for entering the employ of the company or for agreeing to restrictions in the future. An employee may be asked to say that he will never leave the company and therefore the employer would have the use of that employee's services as long as he wanted them; the employee could not go over to one of his competitors.
Income Tax Act
That might be a boomerang.

It might or might not be, I am not in position to say. The ordinary little taxpayer or employee of a company would not get things like this; it is only the top executives who are in positions of control who could arrange anything like this. It is to prevent that practice of regarding these things as though they were not actually payments for services.
Would the normal gift of cash at Christmastime to an employee be included in the employee's income?

Christmas bonuses are
regarded as income. After all, they are part of the emoluments received by the employee for services rendered.
Could a gift be considered as something apart from a bonus?

The only reason an employer would make a gift at Christmas or any other time during the year to an employee would be as a return for faithful service, and after all that would be part of his income whether it was paid monthly or given as a gift.
What if it were in kind rather than in cash?
I am informed that the value of the gift is regarded as income.

Supposing when we leave here at Christmas we give a pair of gloves or some flowers to the secretaries who work for us, would the departmental officials regard that for one moment as being income? Surely nothing so nonsensical could be suggested?
My hon. friend, who is a lawyer, will be able to give me the answer in Latin which I have been given.

What the parliamentary assistant is saying is that we are not their employers as individuals. Let us go back to the private companies and see if we can get a smart answer to that. The last line of the resolution reads:
-remuneration for services or consideration for restrictions on the activities of the employee.
I thought I understood the reply given a few moments ago, but I want to be sure. What this means is that any transfer of money or anything of value between an employer and employee is in fact income and the individual would be charged for that. Is that not the law now? I cannot see that this adds anything to the present law. 1 am working for somebody and he gives me so much money or so many potatoes or something else in kind. That is all regarded as income. It must be if

Income Tax Act
Christmas bonuses are so regarded. I am utterly unable to see why we should have this conglomeration of words which will only confuse the simple law as it is today. Perhaps my judgment is wrong about that, but that is the way it appears to me.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Carried.
With great respect to another parliamentary assistant who does not understand it and who probably will not even though he keeps shouting "carried"-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: With great respect, I am not saying anything about the law.
The parliamentary assistant said "carried". I heard him and I want to congratulate him on being so bright.

The point I tried to make earlier was that attempts have been made here similar to those in the United States to treat these things as capital payments which are made, not for services rendered but for other reasons. A payment might be made for an employee agreeing never to work for another employer, to restrict his future activities, and it was challenged that such a payment was not income. To make it quite clear that these things would be regarded as income a clause will be inserted in the bill which perhaps my hon. friend will be able to follow much better.

I am all right up to the beginning of the proviso, but I should like the parliamentary assistant to explain the proviso, which reads:
-unless it is established that they cannot reasonably be regarded as consideration for entry into the employment, remuneration for services or consideration for restrictions on the activities of the employee.
Could the parliamentary assistant give examples for each of these provisos? The first is that moneys paid cannot reasonably be regarded as consideration for entry into the employment. I should like an example of that. The second is remuneration for services or consideration for restrictions on the activities of the employee. I should also like an example of that. It is so involved that I doubt whether the appeal board would be able to interpret what it means. Possibly if examples are given we can understand it.

Perhaps I should first point out that the legal draftsmanship is certainly not mine, nor am I competent to interpret it. As far as the grammar is concerned, I would point out there is a double negative, and I would take it that the double negative means that these things are going to be regarded as

income. If they are anything else they are not income, but these things are. An example of the first one would be a person taking a bonus of $10,000 to begin employment with a company, in addition to his regular salary.
Would that be free of income tax?

No, that is income. Any one of these things which are mentioned is going to be regarded as income. I must confess that if I were a lawyer I would have used the direct approach, but the double negative means if any one of these things was the reason why the capital payment was made, then that capital payment is income. If, on the other hand, it should happen that an employer had to buy a piece of property belonging to an employee, that would be a perfectly normal transaction. It is not covered by the last two lines and therefore it is not income.

What would be an
example of the second proviso?

A straight bonus for entering service at all. Perhaps a good example of the first one would be the case of hockey and football players who are given say $10,000 to begin with in return for entering into a contract for their services with one hockey or baseball club.
Is that what it is to cover?
That is one of the things.
In view of the explanation of the parliamentary assistant as to the drafting, would it be correct to say that in drafting a law of this kind when the lawyers want to say yes they say "no, no"?

I have one more question as a matter of information, because I often hear it referred to. Suppose a person were employed by a limited company with a salary of $10,000 a year, and collected no part of his salary for a period of three years. Suppose he then discharged his liability to the company, the amount of $30,000, by selling his contract of service back to the company for $20,000. Would that be subject to income tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In this particular instance I think it would be considered as income. It discharges a debt for a salary, which salary would have been taxable in ordinary circumstances. Every year the salary of $10,000 would have been taxable. At the end of three years the amount due is $30,000. A settlement is made for $20,000. The $20,000, being in settlement of previously earned salary, is taxable.
It is taxable?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is.

Just one question, and I promise I will not rise again. I wonder if you should not have some restriction after the word "activities" as, for example, "activities in the interests of the employee". It seems to me you leave yourself wide open on the word "activities". Surely it is presumed it would be activities from which the employer benefits, or something of that kind. It occurred to me you might want to do something about that in the act. You might just look at that.
Of course this is only the resolution. When we come to the bill the language will be clear.	-
I merely make the suggestion that when we come to the bill it might be advisable to restrict it.

On September 29 the hon. member for Macleod, I believe it was, asked a question whether payment for the services of an ambulance would be included in the exemptions, and the minister said that he did not think so. I said at that time that I thought if a doctor included in his bill the charge for the ambulance it could be deducted from the man's income tax. Will the parliamentary assistant say whether, if the ambulance charge is included in the doctor's account, it can be deducted from the individual's income tax?
Before I answer a hypothetical question, what reason would there be for a doctor to include an ambulance bill in his account?
He might own an ambulance.
He might be an undertaker, too.

There are cases where some one party is unable to pay at the time. There are doctors who have themselves paid the charge for the ambulance, and perhaps six or seven months later have collected the amount from the individual.

I can only refer the hon. member to section 26 of the Income Tax Act which gives in detail the medical charges permitted as a deduction. I am told by the medical authorities around me that they know of no case where a doctor owns an ambulance.

That was suggested on this side of the house. The doctor behind you likely told you that, but I know of two cases where the doctor has had to pay the ambulance charges, and six or seven months afterwards has collected it.

I have heard of cases in Ireland where the doctor made his visits in a hearse so that if he was not successful or if he arrived too late he would save the family expense, but I have not heard of doctors in Canada assuming the responsibility for the ambulance charge.

It is quite all right when a question is asked for the parliamentary assistant to read the act and say that is what is in the act. This afternoon, when we were talking about another tax, he said that people should know it is in the act. If the people should know certainly we should know. Therefore why does he say, "There is the act; it is in the act"? We know it is in the act. What we want is to have it taken out of the act. What we want is to have the act changed so that ambulance fees will be regarded as medical expenses. That is the point.
We should like to have some statement from him as to whether or not the government thinks it is reasonable to have ambulance fees included as a medical expense. The case I have in mind is that of a man who had to travel 200 miles in an ambulance to get special attention. His wife went with him. They had to put up at a hotel for a night before he could get a room in the hospital. He applied for exemption for those charges. I can understand if he had to go to a hotel perhaps that in itself would not involve a medical expense. I know the government would run into some difficulty and perhaps discover there were a lot of travellers who had been taken sick when they had to stay at a hotel. I can understand the hotel part not being included as medical expenses, but for the life of me I cannot understand why ambulance charges are not included in medical expenses. When one travels a couple of hundred miles by ambulance, the bill is considerable. I believe such charges should be included in medical expenses if the patient has to be transported to some place for medical attention. If the officials are doubtful about the charge, a statement from the doctor could be secured.
I believe an ambulance charge is a legitimate claim for exemption, and I should like the department to tell us whether or not they think so; and if so, will they have it changed?

In answer to the initial remarks of the hon. member, may I say that the member for Peterborough West asked me

Income Tax Act
whether there was a provision in the act, and I did give him the actual section of the act. So far as the question of the member for Macleod is concerned, consideration has been given to allowing other than medical expenses, but at this time it is not government policy to extend these concessions further.
I asked the parliamentary assistant whether an ambulance charge could be included in the doctor's bill, and be exempted in that way.
No.

I had no intention of entering the discussion on this resolution, but if the department gives favourable consideration to the request which has been put forward, and perhaps with justification, for those who are fortunate enough to be able to travel via ambulance, will they also kindly remember the transportation charges which have to be met in a district such as mine where a man has to hire a plane and travel 500 or 600 miles to reach a doctor. I do not intend to hold up the committee for any length of time, but I do not intend to let the people who are fortunate enough to be able to ride in an ambulance at a cost of $5 or $10 go to the department with that request and have it granted, without some consideration being given to those people who have to hire an aeroplane, which is an item of real expense.

My reply to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat is that even though a patient had to take a train, upon the doctor's insistence in writing, then that expense should be allowed. It does not make any difference.
I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant whether it is not correct that the income tax department does allow ambulance charges now?
The answer is no.
I would suggest that the parliamentary assistant ask the Minister of National Revenue, because I know of cases where ambulance charges have been allowed.

Speaking about these ambulance charges, I should like to say that on numerous occasions in my district people

Mr. Chairman,-

As to deep-test wells, I think the parliamentary assistant probably has not the full information in the matter.

If a company or an individual is going to drill a well in these areas where great depth is required, because the distance may be twice as great, the time taken to drill the well, instead of being twice as long, may be four or five times as long. Has the

basis as other concessions so that people who may be willing to do that drilling may have greater incentive.
