speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, November 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gardiner for the second reading of Bill No. 147, to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL COMPENSATION TO OWNERS OF SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when eleven o'clock came on Monday evening we were discussing this bill and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) had asked me for the date of a certain presentation made to the minister last spring. I now find it was Tuesday, March 15, 1949. I had intended to refer only to a paragraph or two of the presentation that was made, but in view of some of the things that have happened it might be well to place the whole presentation on the record at this time. It reads:
Representing cattle raisers in a group of western Ontario counties we desire to make certain representations to you and the government concerning compensation for reactors under the T.B. area test.
With the broad principle of T.B. testing and the eradication of bovine tuberculosis we are in full accord. The altered economy of the nation makes the present compensation for reactors entirely inadequate and imposes upon the loser of cattle an unfair share of the costs.
Obviously, compensation is a recognition of responsibility on the part of the state, or the public at large. The eradication of bovine tuberculosis is manifestly a public health enterprise and it is only fair that the state should share in the price that must be paid.
Under health of animals regulations obtaining up to world war II, compensation and salvage values combined to reimburse the cattle raiser to a fair extent, clean-up costs were not excessive and herds could be replaced at or around the reimbursement figures.
Then came the war. T.B. testing was discontinued and a group of counties in western Ontario which applied for the test in the late thirties are now being tested under altogether different conditions. The whole economy of the nation has changed. Cattle values have risen. All costs have multiplied and the compensation, always modest, but over long periods perhaps fair, now represents a much smaller portion of the loss.
Under present conditions the cattle raiser is compelled to bear a much larger share of the cost of this great public health enterprise. The state,

Animal Contagious Diseases Act in other words the people whose health is safeguarded by this testing program, pay a much smaller share of the cost.
In view of the magnificent war record of Canadian agriculture we cannot be convinced that the people of Canada will demand that farmers in the newly tested areas, and in areas still to be tested, shall be classed as "war casualties" and made to bear this unfair share of a post-war public health project.
Net losses are ranging from a few hundred dollars up to three and four thousand dollars. There are cases of young farmers, just getting started who have lost their entire herds, and some of these young men borrowed money to purchase the animals that have now gone to the slaughter house. Not only have they lost their herds, but they must now bear the expense of a thorough clean-up; it will cost a great deal of money, at present values, to buy in a similar number of cattle of comparable quality and the monthly cheque for milk and dairy products is forfeited until the herd is replaced.
Young farmers exposed to such a set of circumstances have commendable courage and determination if they carry on.
Middle-aged farmers are in a similar position, except that their net losses are usually much greater because of larger herds built up over the years. They, too, have fortitude and determination if they proceed to rebuild.
The situation is indeed serious-in some cases tragic. The $38 received as compensation is a ridiculously small recognition, or reward, on the part of the state, when the cattle raiser is obliged to pay $250 or $300 for cattle as good as those sacrificed in this T.B. clean-up campaign.
The inadequacy of the compensation can be further emphasized by the fact that after compensation and salvage have been received many cattle raisers suffer a net loss of two and three thousand dollars. Surely the people of Canada are not demanding that sacrifice on the part of Canadian farmers.
We submit that the regulations are too rigid. Appraisal values are now far too low and the actual compensation is grossly inadequate in these times.
More flexible regulations, with an element of adaptability about them, might be found applicable even to the circumstances about which we complain.
Recommendations
We submit that the valuation on grade cows should be raised to $100 with a comparable increase in the valuation placed on other classes of cattle.
Perhaps the severest blow is suffered by farmers in the loss of cattle going to the tank and thus, under present regulations, producing no salvage revenue. We therefore strongly urge that market value at prevailing beef prices be paid the owner, as well as compensation, for all animals declared to be tankers.
And we recommend further that these increased payments be made retroactive to the beginning of post-war area testing.
Some time later the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and his parliamentary assistant made certain statements. The parliamentary assistant is reported on page 2737 of Hansard of April 29, 1949, as having answered a question asked by Mr. Daniel, the former member for Oxford, as follows:
I can assure the member that it is the intention of the government to increase the compensation paid to T.B. reactors, and also to make it retroactive.

The Minister of Agriculture is reported at page 2239 of Hansard of April 1, 1949, as having said:
I am able to state that those who are concerned with the matter have been in to see us and they did not ask for any more than we were considering giving, so I think it likely there will be satisfaction when an announcement is finally made.
A group of cattle raisers approached the department and following that the minister and his parliamentary assistant made the promises that I have referred to. This bill certainly does not live up to those promises; the promises and the practices are poles apart. In the statement made by the parliamentary assistant no reference whatever was made to tankers; the only reference was to reactors.
In legal matters a great deal of attention is paid to precedent and I should like to direct attention to the precedents that have been established by former ministers of agriculture under similar conditions, and I refer to the Hon. Mr. Burrell in 1913, the Hon. Mr. Crerar in 1918, and the Hon. Mr. Motherwell in 1923, as well as the Hon. Mr. Tolmie, who was minister of agriculture when the original motion was introduced to take care of the problems covered by this bill.
This being a money bill, I am not in position to introduce an amendment, but, as I have mentioned previously, many farmers in the counties of Oxford, Norfolk, Perth and others are disappointed. I should like to refer to one or two statements that have been made in the house on previous occasions. First I should like to quote a statement made by the late Harry Leader, former member for Portage la Prairie, as reported on page 2739 of Hansard of 1922. He said:
I wish to protest against the reduction of the indemnity paid for purebred cattle. I have received numerous letters and telegrams and I know if I stay here long enough I shall be beseiged by sheaves of letters and telegrams in regard to this matter.
Breeders are just waking up to the fact that there is going to be a reduction in the indemnity.
That was in 1922 when the government was trying to reduce the amount. If they thought it convenient to reduce it when cattle prices were going down, then surely they can find it convenient to increase it when cattle prices are much higher. Mr. Leader went on to say:
I protest against the reduction in the indemnifications for cattle . . . But what about the effect of the disease on human beings? The statistics show that one child, in every three under the age of ten who have tuberculosis, contacted the disease through a bovine origin.
It is my opinion that the work should be continued, and that farmers should not be discouraged but encouraged. Mr. Kellner, a member of the house in 1922, produced statistics to show that the average value of a grade cow in the province of Ontario was $59, and

at the same time the valuation for compensation purposes was placed at $150 for pure-breds and $60 for grades, the government paying two-thirds of those figures. Therefore I feel that the bill is not adequate and I should like to hear the parliamentary assistant explain why it is so inadequate.

subtopic: ADDITIONAL COMPENSATION TO OWNERS OF SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
Before the motion carries, Mr. Speaker, there is one matter I want to put before the parliamentary assistant. I have raised this question time after time in the house. I brought it up again during the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in the present session. It has to do with two of the most glaring cases that agriculture has experienced in the matter of compensation paid for reactors under the tuberculosis test regulations. I regret that it is necessary to raise the subject so often, but when I was on my feet on the last occasion I cautioned the minister in connection with it, and said that I thought there was a sufficiently outstanding injustice perpetrated upon these two particular farmers and dairymen for the matter to be repeated until some remedy was provided.
The reason I am raising it again is that the principle of Bill 147 seems to be aimed not at remedying the injustice but at preventing the government from remedying it. I am not going to refer to clauses of the bill because that normally takes place in committee. One of the major principles of the bill is in section 3, and as I see it it prevents any review, unless the parliamentary assistant can give an explanation in committee to the contrary, or any payment of compensation to these farmers whose cause I have tried to champion before.
In order that the parliamentary assistant may understand the point I am raising, in a year previous to 1947, prior to which the act is not retroactive, Donald McIntyre, a farmer and dairyman living a little to the east of Stayner in the county of Simcoe, had a herd of purebred Holstein cattle which had been tested for tuberculosis for years and years under the ordinary government regulations, and had always reacted favourably. In the year 1943 or 1944-I am not sure which it is, but it is on record so often that it is easy to ascertain-forty-three out of forty-four of his herd went down and were slaughtered. When they went to the abattoir there was not a single jot or tittle of evidence that any of them had tuberculosis anywhere in their carcasses.
In addition to that, a careful examination was made by the government veterinarians at the abattoir, and the closest they could come to any sign of tuberculosis was that there was evidence that at one time one cow had had pneumonia. To me that seemed to *	45781-1054
Animal Contagious Diseases Act be stretching it pretty far, and the farmer took a similar view of it. I am told that at that particular time-and I do not think there is any doubt about the evidence in this case- there was a change in the type of serum used in the tuberculosis test. I know that changes have been made in the serum from time to time, and the department no doubt would readily explain that they were made because of certain United States regulations. Sometimes some of our cattle have been allowed to go there, and it was found when they got them there that the United States serum showed an unfavourable reaction, and that the cows were reactors.
Nevertheless, in the case to which I have referred a new serum was used, a serum that apparently was particularly severe on the system of the animal, and it caused the whole herd to go down with the exception of one cow. The veterinarians involved in the matter were not satisfied. I am satisfied also that the department was greatly concerned about what had happened. Not only did one herd go down but also another herd in the province of Nova Scotia reacted at the same time, and that farmer also lost his cattle. I think it can be established beyond any question that the serum used, severe as it was, caused these farmers to lose their herds, and to have to take a lower price by virtue thereof.
It seems to me that the act will be an insurmountable obstacle to any review or payment which might be made to these two badly used farmers. It is not as though there are hundreds of herds across Canada for which compensation will have to be paid because of the severity of this particular serum. So far as I know, and I think the records of the department will bear me out, there are only two herds. Time after time we have done things in this house to provide for special cases. Where the fault does not lie with the farmer but with the government, I think the government has a special obligation that ought to be met. I hope that the parliamentary assistant, when he comes to section 3 of the bill, will not say that the legislation rules out a review of these cases. I had hoped, from the rather favourable reaction of the minister when his estimates were before the house, that he was going to give favourable consideration to remedying this most outstanding injustice. It is a great disappointment and discouragement to me, as it is to the two farmers involved, that legislation such as this should be put on the statute books which will block the possibility of remedying an injustice. What we should be doing is passing statutes to remedy injustices, not putting on the statute books of Canada laws that will prevent injustices from

Animal Contagious Diseases Act being remedied. I do plead with the parliamentary assistant to see that, whatever happens with respect to this legislation, it does not bar the correcting of abuses such as I have outlined.
I said before, and I repeat, that neither of these two farmers is a constituent of mine. I have no axe to grind, but I have been impressed with the obvious injustice-I am not suggesting that the government was trying to get reactors among those herds, but wherever there may be some doubt the government ought to lean towards the farmer. I believe the government should pay the farmer for the loss that was occasioned through no fault of his, but owing to the fact that the serum used was too severe. As I understand, this serum was later withdrawn.
Now, that is the case in a nutshell. I regret having to raise this question time after time, but I will say, Mr. Speaker, that I intend to raise it until such time as that injustice is remedied. If this bill is going to bar the remedying of that situation, then the minister ought to review it before it finally becomes law. It is not fair; it is not just; it is not equitable. Surely, if there is any class of people in Canada deserving of justice and equity, it is the people in our agricultural sections.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to register my protest in regard to the compensation offered in this bill. I believe the parliamentary assistant and the minister know quite well that it is not sufficient. The promises which were made before the election campaign are not being fulfilled. I believe the minister should listen to the protests that have been made. The test is being conducted in my county now, and many farmers are complaining about the amount they are receiving.
I might mention one woman in particular who, before the election, wrote to me complaining about the fact that her cattle were the only cattle that reacted in that particular section. She complained bitterly. I do not know why her cattle were the only ones. It might have been that they were the only affected cattle in the section because, certainly, I do not believe any difference would be made in the tests. Apparently, she thought she was being discriminated against, and it was rather difficult to talk her out of that position. In any event, the compensation being offered in this bill is not nearly sufficient to pay for the loss sustained when cattle react to the test.
Those members who know something about keeping a dairy herd are well aware of what it costs to replenish a herd. Many herds have reacted; in some sections worse than in others. My own herd has not yet been tested,
[Mr. Graydon.l

so I am not talking about myself. I do plead with the parliamentary assistant to do everything he can to have this bill sent to a committee and re-worded, so that those who have suffered losses will receive fair compensation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: ADDITIONAL COMPENSATION TO OWNERS OF SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the question raised by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Murray), I should say that that question will be answered when the bill goes to the committee. It was not my intention to say very much about this bill at this time, but owing to what has been said I feel it is my duty, as parliamentary assistant, to say something about the matter.
This question has been under discussion since last fall. Last October or November, when the federation meetings were being held in the county of Middlesex, this matter was brought to the fore quite forcibly. The feeling at the township meetings in the county of Middlesex was that the farmers were not receiving fair compensation for the reactors. I attended many of those meetings and listened to the suggestions, both pro and con, about what should be done. I was questioned about it and I asked questions of those present. I obtained the views of the farmers of my own county as best I could. There were views put forward in favour of raising the compensation for reactors, and other views in favour of raising the compensation for the reactors that went to the tank.
I listened to all those views, and considered them for some time. I came to Ottawa in December of last year, at the time of the dominion-provincial conference on agriculture, and took this matter up with our departmental officials. I asked them if some assistance could not be given the farmers who lost cattle as a result of these T.B. tests. They asked me what I wanted to do, and I said I should like to have the Animal Contagious Diseases Act amended. As such an amendment would have to be brought before parliament and parliament

was not meeting until January, nothing could be done until that time. I asked the departmental officials to consider the matter in the meantime.
As I said, the federation had met in Middlesex county. During the meeting, resolutions were passed and I have copies of those resolutions. Most of the resolutions did not request as much as we are now granting, but the resolutions differed from township to township. When parliament met in January of this year, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the officials of the department discussed this matter. We were all of the same opinion as to what should be done for those farmers who had lost cattle as a result of the T.B. tests. Everyone in this house understands that these T.B. tests are for health purposes.
Some of the farmers are opposed to the test, just as I was back in 1939. At that time a petition was circulated in the county of Middlesex for these T.B. tests, and I was one of those bitterly opposed to it. I am not opposed to it now. I feel it is a proper move to make. The sooner our herds are cleaned up, the better. We discussed what should be done, and various ideas were expressed. The departmental officials were requested to make a survey to ascertain how much it would cost if an amendment to the act were introduced to raise the compensation to the price mentioned in the act, $60 and $150, instead of two-thirds of that amount. The survey was made and we were told what the cost would be.
During that period of time, the federation of agriculture sent a deputation to Ottawa to interview the minister and departmental officials about raising the compensation. They did not come alone. They got in touch with the surrounding counties of Middlesex, Oxford, Elgin, Lambton, Kent, Perth and Huron; and on March 15 representatives came from all those counties I have just mentioned, except Oxford. Oxford did not send a representative down on that occasion. But the other men came down. Before they came, they had discussed this matter with me or our own men of Middlesex county; and they appointed two men to come down. These were level-headed young chaps who were interested in this T.B. testing, for they both had had their own herds tested and had lost quite a few cattle by it. They came down and interviewed the minister and myself with respect to this matter.
What the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) has read is the brief that they handed to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) on that occasion. The minister had discussed this matter at length with myself and with the officials. We had come to an
Animal Contagious Diseases Act agreement on it. I will take part of the responsibility for that. We felt that the best plan to follow was to pay the full price for the T.B. reactors that went to the tanks and leave the compensation what it was; that was $100 and $40. I am taking the actual amounts. I am not taking the two-thirds that is being paid. You understand that the amount was set at $60 for grades and $150 for purebreds; but we paid only two-thirds of that amount. We felt it was better to leave that amount of compensation at $40 for grade cattle and $100 for purebred cattle and to raise the amount that was paid for the T.B. reactors that went to the tank.
To the representatives of the federation who came to us on that occasion we told what we intended to do. I can tell you this, Mr. Speaker. The representatives of all those counties did not raise a dissenting voice. They said they were heartily in favour of the action we were taking. There was not much said. They asked that it be retroactive, but not much was said with respect to how far back it would go. But they went away perfectly satisfied. As I said before, I was sitting right there in the room and I did not hear one dissenting voice raised from among them.
Then we went ahead and prepared a bill in the early part of March, and our officials determined the amount of money that it would cost the dominion treasury if we followed out the policy that we had inaugurated; that was, leaving the compensation the way it was, $40 and $100, and paying the full cost of the T.B. reactors that went to the tank.
They came back with a bill prepared, and giving us the cost to the dominion treasury, saying that that act would go into effect on the first day of April of this year. You know full well that I would oppose that suggestion most strenuously. I felt that was unfair to the numerous counties and sections of the country across Canada. If we brought that bill into effect on the first of April, those that were tested before the first of April would not benefit by it, but only those that were tested after the first of April. We asked that they endeavour to make it retroactive to the time we struck upon, April 1, 1947, which was a time when we felt there was quite a bit of T.B. testing done after the war.
They then had to scrap that bill, and go ahead and make a survey of what it was going to cost to make it retroactive. You understand, Mr. Speaker, as does the house, that that would take a good deal of time. But nevertheless our officials went ahead and prepared that bill. They went ahead and told us approximately how much it was going to cost and how much money we would have to ask the dominion treasury for. As you know, our minister was in the west in the
1652	HOUSE OF
Animal Contagious Diseases Act latter part of April, and on April 29 that bill was handed to me. As you know, we dissolved on the next day. I had the bill in my pocket when the question was asked by the then member for Oxford and the then member for Bruce, when they rose in their seats across the floor of the house and asked the question that has just been read from Hansard of April 29. I made the answer that the compensation would be raised. I was sincere in that answer. I was not asked to give an explanation of it. I only said what I knew was going to take place. The hon. member for Bruce put the question to me. It will be found in Hansard of that date. I do not need to look it up; I have it here on my desk. He asked me if that would be made retroactive to the fall of 1947 and my answer was that when the bill was brought down it would be satisfactory to the good people of Bruce on that occasion; for I knew that they had not started in testing before the first of April, 1947.
That was the condition up to that date. Of course, I felt worried about this bill. I was keenly interested in it because the farmers of Canada were interested in it; and anything that is of interest to the farmers of Canada, Mr. Speaker, is of interest to me.
As I felt that the house was going to dissolve the next day and that we were going to go to the country, and as I felt keenly about that bill, 1 went to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and asked him if there would be a chance for me to introduce it before the house dissolved. He said that there would not, but that he would give me his word that if we were returned to power he would see to it that the bill was introduced at the first session after the election. I made that answer across the floor of the house, and you know the answer that came back, Mr. Speaker. I was hooted for that statement; for hon. members opposite felt that neither the Prime Minister nor I would have the opportunity of introducing any bill after the election. But you know what took place on June 27.
That was the condition up to that time.
I will say this, Mr. Speaker. That question was made a political football all during the election campaign. I have some of the advertisements of my worthy opponents at that time, and I know what they said. It has been stated that outside the house, with respect to this matter, I had made statements that were not true and not in accordance with the facts. I can read numerous reports, but I will read one which is from the London Free Press of May 7, when I was speaking in Seaforth at the convention that chose the present member for Huron-Perth, Mr. 

McLean. I was speaking at that convention. Here is my statement then. This was taken from the London Free Press of May 7:
There had been some criticism, said Mr. McCubbin, that the compensation paid for T.B. reactors that went to the tank was insufficient. The Prime Minister had promised that if his government was returned that the cattle producers would get full value as if the animal had gone for beef.
That is exactly my statement on that occasion. I will take another statement that I made, addressing my own nomination meeting at Strathroy; and if there are any people that I would never fool, they are my own people. I made the same statement to them. I said that, if this government was returned, a bill would be introduced with respect to compensation for T.B. reactors, and that I would see that the full cost would be paid for the T.B. reactors that went to the tank. I made that quite clear. On every occasion on which I spoke at that time I mentioned T.B. reactors that went to the tank. Nevertheless, you know what took place.
Here are some of the advertisements of my opponents. Here is the picture of my friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), and here is a whole page with respect to T.B. reactors, and with respect to what I said on that occasion. This advertisement appears in The Ledger of London, Ontario, and contains these words:
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture sought to whitewash this deliberate refusal to rule upon a matter so important to you. by promising to do better in the future.
What I have promised, I have just told you. In all the addresses I made in western Ontario I promised that the full beef prices would be paid for the T.B. reactors that went to the tank. I felt-and I have not changed my mind-that the fairest way to deal with this matter was as follows. The farmer has a cow, a heifer or a steer. The animal is sent to the abattoir and killed. He should get the beef value of that animal. The farmer needs to be careful with this. We know the farmers are shrewd and careful. If they send the beast to the abattoir they will get the full beef value. If the beast is infected and goes to the tank they get only the hide value. If it is not infected they will get the full beef value.
I know what the farmers in my district are receiving for these cattle that are sent to the abattoirs. These are not tankers. They get the beef value plus $38 or $40. They are well satisfied with this price. The farmer who has a T.B. reactor which goes to the tank is not satisfied now and has not been satisfied. He receives only the price of the hide, which is $6 or $8 or whatever it happens to be, plus $38 or $40. If that farmer

should receive the full beef price for the T.B. reactor I can tell the house that he would be satisfied. In my contacts with the farmers of western Ontario I have never heard one say that he was not satisfied.
The hon. member for Brant-Wentworth (Mr. Charlton) made the statement that he has not heard anyone who complained about the T.B. reactors that went to the tank. That has not been my experience. That is the man who has kicked very strongly. Hon. members will say to me: Why are you doing this? What precedent have you for this? I can tell them that there is no country in the world-and I am taking in the whole wide world-that does as much for T.B. reactors as Canada does. Take the United States. Hon. members understand the set-up there. The veterinary and a valuator come in and value the beef. Take a cow. The cow is worth $200. That is the valuation the valuator places upon it. He sends the T.B. reactor to the abattoir as a farmer in Canada would do. Say he receives $150 for the beef in that cow. Then he is paid one-third of the difference between the beef price and the valuator's price. That would be one-third of $50. Hon. members can figure that out for themselves. It will be $15 or $16. Hon. members may ask me, What about the T.B. reactor that goes to the tank? It is not worth anything as beef. The same thing takes place there. The valuation placed upon that cow or beef may be $200. He would receive $10 for the hide, and he would receive one-third of $190. Hon. members can figure that out for themselves. As a matter of fact it is $62 or $63. That is the amount of money that he would receive.
The over-all picture in the United States is as follows:	The average amount that the
federal Department of Agriculture pays across the whole country does not exceed $25 per head. I claim that we in Canada are doing the thing that is fairest to all the farmers, and that is the only way to act with them. I know that there will be the individual case as was mentioned by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon). I shall answer that when we get into committee. I feel that we are doing the fair thing by the farmers of Canada, and that is what we should do. If there is any class of people in this country who should receive due and honest consideration it is the farmers.

speechtext:
I should like to interject a somewhat different note into this discussion. Looking at section 1 it would appear that our old friend the horse, or at least his owner, is going to take a beating. The section to be repealed provided for the payment of $150 for each grade horse and $300 for each purebred, but under the proposed amendment the payments will be at the rate of $100 and $200 respectively, a considerable decrease.
I imagine that the reason that was done is that the ordinary work animal on the farm is fast disappearing and in a few years there will probably be none left except in the isolated areas. Perhaps that is the reason for the reduction in payments. At the present time the grade horse, or even the purebred draft horse, brings a small price in comparison to what was obtained ten, fifteen or twenty years ago. On the other hand, light horses have been increasing in price and as far as I can see the only horse that is going to be bred in this or other countries is the light type of thoroughbred, standard bred and saddle horse.
The number of people who are riding horses has increased in recent years rather than decreased and the demand for good saddle horses is better today than it has been for many years. The type of horse that we sold for $25 to $50 in 1920 in western Canada now brings from $100 to $300. In other words, while the price of draft horses has been coming down, the price of light horses has been going up. Therefore, it would seem to be a mistake to reduce the compensation to be paid for animals destroyed under this act.
I think the parliamentary assistant knows that the thoroughbred or standard bred horse is worth more than it was twenty years ago and is worth even more than the compensation provided in the old section. The same applies to animals which are not registered, such as saddle horses. In order to protect the light horse breeders the compensation provided in the old section should be continued.
